articles.title: What Cedric Robinson’s Black Marxism Gets Wrong
articles.author: August H. Nimtz
articles.content: Cedric Robinson’s Black Marxism: The Making of the Black Radical Tradition did not receive widespread attention after its original publication in 1983. Since 2000, when it was republished with a new preface and an introduction by historian Robin D. G. Kelley, however, the book has enjoyed widespread appeal and influence in the anglophone humanities and social sciences as well as among activists. Robinson’s proposed theory of “racial capitalism” and his framework of a “black radical tradition” have shaped debates about racial inequalities in capitalist societies and Marxism’s potential for anti-racist politics in recent decades. August Nimtz has engaged with the book’s arguments and trajectory, directly or indirectly, since its original publication. The recently published collection , Black Marxism: A Marxist Critique , makes accessible, for the first time, a critique that spans four decades and addresses Robinson’s claims and those made by his followers by putting forth an authentic Marxism as the most reliable method for human liberation in the real world and explaining why it remains the guiding principle for the transracial class struggle today. Constantin Berlin You recently said that your book has been in the making for over forty years. Indeed, your examination of Robinson’s book began with a critical review, published in 1984. What’s motivated you to have your original review essay of Robinson’s book reprinted, to republish two other related essays, and to write a new review? Why now? August H. Nimtz Context — the political moment in which we now live. Virtually all of my writings, beginning with my 2000 Marx and Engels: Their Contribution to the Democratic Breakthrough , are informed by historical context. They all constitute, in one way or another, a political intervention into the moment in which they are written. When the Stalinist regimes in Russia and Eastern Europe were unraveling and no longer claiming to be Marxist, I thought that it would be an opportune moment to make the case for the real Marxist project, specifically its democratic essence. Great , I said to myself, the Stalinists were no longer pretending to be what they never were . But I had difficulty finding a publisher. The not-so-subtle message from left publishers was “You’re swimming against the tide; the Marxist project is history,” as confirmed, apparently, by what had taken place a decade earlier with the regimes that claimed to be Marxist. After many rejection letters, I finally found a publisher, a mainstream academic one. In contrast, as I’ve since thought about it, Robinson, it appears, had little difficulty in finding a new publisher for his 1983 Black Marxism , which had been largely ignored for more than a decade. He found a receptive audience who also believed that [Karl] Marx’s project was a spent force, a has-been, confined to the proverbial dustbin of history. Robinson’s book, which rejected the real Marx despite its duplicitous title, seemed to offer an explanation: Marx’s supposedly mistaken assumption about the revolutionary potential of the proletariat and his alleged Eurocentrism. My starting point today is that, in the era of [Donald] Trump and what he represents, the last thing progressive forces need is a project that claims to be revolutionary, more revolutionary than what Marx had to offer, but is really a chimera and thus dangerous for that reason. A “wholly original theory of revolution,” according to historian Robin Kelley, with whom I respectfully disagree. Thus the need to critique Robinson, especially now. Constantin Berlin As you suggest, Robinson’s book is now highly regarded, but you were quite critical of it in your 1984 critique, the first detailed appraisal of a book that did not receive much attention when it was first published. Why was that and what did you find problematic with it? August H. Nimtz First, a bit of background. For more than a decade, there had been a bitter debate within US black nationalist circles about the relative merits of a cultural nationalist versus a class analytic approach to black politics. I had a front-row seat to those debates and actively participated in them. A few nights ago, in fact, in a Zoom session about Cuba, specifically the revolution’s unfinished business toward racial equality, I was reminded about those debates. The encounter reminded me of the fact that not many of us who participated in them are still alive, and those of us who are have an obligation to correctly recount them, including the views of those with whom we disagreed. In 1984, the editor of the London-based Journal of African Marxists , who I knew from graduate school and who in turn learned that I was a public Marxist, a member of the US Socialist Workers Party (SWP), asked me to review Black Marxism — and produce a political intervention, in other words. The fact that it was the London-based Zed Press that published Black Marxism most likely explains why an also London-based venue knew about its debut. The book, which I soon realized in my reading, constituted a sophisticated defense of the cultural nationalist perspective, one that had been informed, though superficially, by the class point of view. The debates required Robinson to know something about the Marxist perspective. But to claim as he did that three major Black figures, W. E. B. DuBois, C. L. R. James, and Richard Wright, had to abandon Marxism to find something more liberatory, a “black radical tradition,” flew, as I knew, in the face of the facts. For example, I had the privilege to attend a presentation that James gave in St Paul, Minnesota, in 1976, I believe, in which he praised some of the historic founders of the SWP, which was of importance for me, having recently joined the party. Why would James say something like that? Because St Paul is the sister city of Minneapolis, the site of arguably the high-water mark of the 1930s workers radicalization in the United States, the 1934 Teamsters strike. It was led by a nucleus of communists that James had been affiliated with, Trotskyists, whites to boot. For a still (though less committed) black nationalist to hear someone with James’s credentials give a shout-out to the SWP helped to legitimize the decision I had made. The correctness of that decision was brought home to me a month ago in São Paulo, Brazil, when a young worker, a subway engineer, came up to me after a talk I had just given in which I referenced the 1934 Teamsters strike vis-à-vis the anti–[Immigration and Customs Enforcement] actions that took place in Minneapolis in early 2026. “Oh, yes,” she said, “Minneapolis 1934, the Teamsters strike,” which she had read about. “I hadn’t made the connection.” Robinson’s false claim about individuals like James having broken with Marxism was one of my major criticisms of the book. I knew better. The other major criticism, in hindsight, was more important. Not only had those three historical figures not rejected Marxism, as Robinson contended — certainly DuBois and James — but there were also more contemporary individuals who embraced Marxism, not the least of whom was Maurice Bishop, the leader of a revolution unfolding in real time in Grenada as Robinson was writing his book. I knew enough at the time about the real Marxist project to reject any perspective that claimed to be revolutionary but failed to see a revolutionary project in real time, especially in the black world that Robinson’s book claimed to be the expert on. Instinctively, I knew Black Marxism to be politically deficient. Maurice Bishop (1944–1983), then–prime minister of Grenada, speaks during a 1979 press conference at the United Nations (Chuck Fishman / Getty Images) Not for naught did I end my 1984 critique with inconvenient advice from Bishop in 1983 to African Americans like Robinson: get over your hang-up about working with white workers — the real issue that had divided cultural nationalists from those of us who subscribed to a Marxist perspective. In hindsight, I was too close in real time to appreciate the full significance of Grenada’s absence in Robinson’s narrative — which I’ve tried to rectify in my new review of his book. A few years ago, I learned, accidentally, that Bishop and I were members, at least on paper, of the same organization, the African Liberation Support Committee. Collating my ALSC files in my office to send them off to an invaluable archive at Michigan State University, I happened to read through the list of various affiliates of the organization in 1973 and noticed for the first time, maybe, that the chapter in Grenada was headed by Bishop, a list on which the Minnesota chapter is included, with me as one of the two contact people. Constantin Berlin In the preface to the new book, you write that you had basically forgotten about your original review until Black Marxism received renewed attention in 2017 through Robin Kelley’s writings. How did this impact your assessment of Robinson’s book? August H. Nimtz Yes, I was surprised to learn, after an extensive Google Scholar search, how influential Robinson’s book had become — which Kelley’s 2017 Boston Review article spoke to. I couldn’t find my 1984 copy and had to retrieve it through Interlibrary Loan. I later found the copy along with relevant correspondence. More surprising were all the accolades being paid to Robinson, given my largely negative reaction. That explained, I soon surmised, why I was mostly unsuccessful in getting it republished — a challenge to the orthodoxy about the book that now prevailed. Except for a Brazilian republication, the uploading of it to the Academia website and a black-politics-oriented podcast, I had little success in bringing attention to what was in fact, as I began to realize, the first detailed treatment of Robinson’s now highly acclaimed book. It took the second coming of Trump to convince me to wage a bit of a campaign to have the 1984 critique republished along with other things I’ve written and a new review of Black Marxism . Thus I’m forever indebted to Michael Yates at Monthly Review Press, editor at the time, for making that possible. The world’s a more dangerous place since Trump’s inauguration in January 2025. It resembles increasingly the lead-up to World War I, a conflagration — the most sanguinary the world had ever seen — that was provoked by capitalist greed,as [Vladimir] Lenin so convincingly argued in the war’s second year in his magisterial Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism . And that it’s Trump who’s leading the charge, naked capitalist greed, unlike the monarchs in 1914, the most authentic capitalist to have ever occupied the White House, couldn’t be more instructive. Tariff and other economic wars can become shooting wars, as World War I taught. But capitalist wars, Marx, [Friedrich] Engels, and Lenin argued, were not inevitable if the working classes take power. Therein the danger of Robinson’s influential book, which consciously dismisses, contra Marx, the proletariat. There is only one force on the planet that can prevent history’s most lethal weapons from being employed to begin World War III and thus the likely end to our species as we know it — namely, the US proletariat. Exactly because Robinson dismissed the American working class and viewed politics through the lens of skin color, his apolitical perspective is the last thing that humanity needs at this moment. Only if the US working class unites in all its identities and constructs a revolutionary workers party can the rest of the world be assured that capital’s inevitable march to World War III won’t happen. My book is a conscious intervention to aid and abet that process. Challenging Robinson’s influential claims constitutes an indispensable task in that campaign. Constantin Berlin Given the other essays in your book, specifically, the 2002 one about the Eurocentric charge regarding Marx’s project, and the 2024 appendix to your coauthored Marx-Douglass comparison, it looks like Robinson has been on your mind for quite some time. Is that accurate? August H. Nimtz I agree, both consciously and unconsciously. By the time I completed doing the research and writing of my 2000 Marx-Engels book ( Marx and Engels: Their Contribution to the Democratic Breakthrough ), I knew far more about their project than I knew in 1984. Robinson’s Eurocentric charge had been on my mind throughout the process, and I included in the final text the evidence to refute it. When the opportunity presented itself to me to sift out the details into a separate essay, I jumped at the opportunity, and thus the essay in the Cambridge University Press 2002 collection (“The Eurocentric Marx and Engels and Other Related Myths” in Marxism, Modernity and Postcolonial Studies ). The most convincing evidence in my opinion to refute the charge was the detailed attention that Marx and Engels gave to the Russian question, a world beyond “the little corner” of the globe, as Marx once sarcastically described Great Britain and Western Europe. I should say, in general, the entire world was Marx’s and Engels’s theater of operation, as the evidence made all so clear. I also learned along the way about another world beyond Europe that they prioritized, “North America,” as they sometimes called it. The US experience, I argue, figured significantly in Marx’s path to communism, one of the major claims of my 2003 Marx, Tocqueville and Race in America . But it was Marx’s response to the Civil War which instantiated, contrary to the implications of Robinson’s Eurocentric charge, that his European origins in no way handicapped him in expertly making sense of the conflagration on the other side of the Atlantic and thus acting efficaciously to be on the right side of history — the liberation of people of African origin from the bondage of chattel slavery. If Robinson were to be believed, what Marx did should have been impossible. A European? I should say that my not-so-hidden agenda when it comes to Marx is to liberate him, as I sometimes say, half-jokingly, from the embrace of political philosophers — sometimes well-meaning — and to bring him back to the world he consciously chose to join in 1843, the world of politics. All my writings home in on his actions, treating his writings as a political act to advance the cause of the proletariat. That’s what my 2000 book does, still the only book-length treatment of Marx as a political activist. It’s worth noting that I wasn’t trained as a political theorist but rather as a political comparativist, which also informs my approach to Marx, who I claim, beginning with his very first publication, had comparativist sensibilities. Note how he was doing comparative jurisprudence, comparing press censor laws in various countries to draw conclusions — which soon motivated him to critique [Georg Wilhelm Friedrich] Hegel on the state. Constantin Berlin This comparative approach also informs your 2024 coauthored book on Karl Marx and Frederick Douglass ( The Communist and the Revolutionary Liberal in the Second American Revolution: Comparing Karl Marx and Frederick Douglass in Real-Time ), from which the appendix is reprinted in your Black Marxism book. Does the chapter inform your new appraisal of Robinson? August H. Nimtz Indeed! The 2024 book is another example of how Robinson was unconsciously on my brain all these years. Though I made no mention of him in the resultant book, Robinson’s Eurocentric charge, as previously mentioned, motivated my first dive into Marx’s Civil War writings. In hindsight, my 2003 Marx, Toqueville, Race book anticipated my 2024 Marx-Douglass comparison. Again, I was trained as a comparativist, not a theorist. That fact is on display in my 2000 Marx-Engels book in which I devoted a chapter to comparing the actions of Marx and Engels on one side of the 1848–49 revolutions and Alexis de Tocqueville on the other side. Making comparisons is arguably the best method we have to test hypotheses in the social sciences. To substantiate my claim that Marx and Engels contributed more than any other figures to the democratic breakthrough in the nineteenth century required some degree of comparison, however minimal. Tocqueville was the best candidate for someone on the other side of the political divide. The evidence revealed that the two communists proved to have had better democratic credentials than the famous author of Democracy in America . In my 2019 book, Marxism versus Liberalism: Comparative Real-Time Political Analysis , I did the same regarding Marx and John Stuart Mill during the US Civil War; again, Marx’s democratic credentials were superior to those of Mill. But Mill, as someone pointed out, was never the activist Marx was and thus I was comparing apples and oranges. When my former undergraduate student, Kyle Edwards, approached me with questions about the abolitionist Frederick Douglass and how he compared to Marx, the light bulb went on. The result was a 417-page book. Marx’s democratic credentials, we discovered, were as good as Douglass’s during the four years of the Civil War. Afterward, we learned they were in fact superior to those of the now former abolitionist. The reason is that for Marx, unlike Douglass, ending chattel slavery was a means to an end rather than an end in itself. Why? To bring into existence a hereditary proletariat for the first time in America, the only class that not only has a class interest in real democracy but also has the capacity to ensure its realization. And when the US working class went into motion for the first time across racial lines, after the war — as Marx would have predicted — Douglass was missing in action, mostly unsupportive. His liberal defense of private property took priority over anything that might have brought about working-class ascendancy — in other words, real democracy. Little did I know that when Robinson republished his 1983 book in 2000, he wrote a new introduction in which he doubled down on his anti-Marxist charges, adding that Marx ignored the question of slavery in America and didn’t relate at all to the abolitionist movement. Only after we completed the Marx-Douglass book did I discover Robinson’s charges. Claims, one might say, that fell right into my lap. The reason: we had just provided the evidence in our book that thoroughly discredited those charges. When the slave oligarchy fired on Fort Sumter in 1861, Marx dropped almost everything to aid and abet Union victory, one of the reasons why his magnum opus, Capital , was never completed. In other words, the 2024 book allowed me to criticize Black Marxism in a far more informed way than was possible forty years earlier. Constantin Berlin You said earlier that the most important problem with Robinson’s book was its political deficiency. Could you elaborate on this? August H. Nimtz Again, when Robinson wrote his book, whose subtitle “The Black Radical Tradition” suggested that it would be about the black revolutionary experience, such an example was underway in real time on the Caribbean island of Grenada and he ignored it — prima facie evidence for me that the book was of little political value. That’s also the reason, I argue, why it was largely ignored for more than a decade. From 1979 to 1989, global politics was characterized by revolutionary upheavals and victories, Grenada, Nicaragua, Iran, Zimbabwe, Angola. Nothing in Robinson’s book, mainly about a timeless and classless “black world,” helped its readers to make sense of that moment. Only later, when revisiting Robinson, did I realize why the Grenada revolution was ignored; it was Marxist inspired. The convergence of the black radical tradition with Marxism was an inconvenient fact for Robinson the cultural nationalist. That also explains why someone else is missing in Black Marxism , which I failed to see in my 1984 reading of the book: Malcolm X. The black nationalist, very publicly, was on a convergence course in the last year of his life with the US Socialist Workers Party, a mostly Caucasian Marxist organization. Robinson, who once hosted Malcolm X at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1963, no doubt knew about that collaboration. Again, an inconvenient fact for him and thus the unpardonable absence of Malcolm X in a book that claimed to be about the “black radical tradition.” Just as important as Malcolm X was the black revolutionary Robert F. Williams, someone who impacted Malcolm X and someone whom Robinson also once invited to speak at Berkeley. Like Malcolm, not coincidentally, Williams also collaborated with the SWP and thus the reason, I contend, why he’s missing in Black Marxism ; another inconvenient fact for a cultural nationalist. Lastly, when Robinson republished his book in 2000, another moment in revolutionary black politics had taken place, the government of Thomas Sankara in Burkina Faso between 1983 and 1987. But Sankara’s name is missing in Robinson’s 2000 introduction. The reason? Sankara, like Bishop, was an unapologetic Marxist — ineligible, therefore, for Robinson’s pantheon of black radicals. Not coincidentally, it’s the US Socialist Workers Party that keeps in print, until today, the speeches of all three black figures, which someone who claimed to be an advocate for the black radical tradition should have applauded. But not so in Robinson’s case. What the examples of Malcolm X, Maurice Bishop, and Thomas Sankara all testify to is the potential for the convergence of revolutionary black nationalism with Marxism — authentic Marxism that is. The more than decade-long debate about the merits of Marxism versus nationalism was being answered in the flesh, which Robinson was unwilling to recognize. I would like to reiterate the point I made earlier: The only force on the planet that can assure that the weapons of mass destruction now in the hands of the US ruling class will not be used in capital’s inevitable march to World War III, and thus the likely end to our species as we know it, is the US proletariat. Thus the importance of finding an answer to the race/class question and forming working class unity in the United States. The example of Malcolm X especially demonstrates that there is indeed a solution to that historical conundrum about working class unity in the United States, the place where the future of our species will be decided. Robinson’s book is an obstacle to clarity on the question. I do everything possible, therefore, to dispute his claims. Too much is at stake not to do so. Thus the reason for my book. For the luck of the genes, I’m one of the few people still alive who participated in those debates and see their historical/political significance. I’d be politically derelict not to make the intervention I intend with the book. Constantin Berlin Lastly, you begin the book with what you call “fortuitous” biography. How did your upbringing shape your politics and ultimately influence your critical reading of Robinson, and why did you include this in the book? August H. Nimtz Yes, my social science/comparativist sensibilities are on full display in that chapter. Given the many similarities in mine and Robinson’s backgrounds, I assumed that many readers of my critique of Black Marxism would wonder how to explain the profound differences between the two of us, especially given the nearly sacrosanct status the book has now achieved, one that I’m now challenging. “Who are you to do so?” they might ask. An interesting puzzle, as we sometimes say in the academic world, that requires an explanation. Comparing our backgrounds might offer one. Robinson’s biography, detailed in Robin Kelley’s foreword to the 2000 republication, is available to the public; mine is not, at least, a version that I’ve had the opportunity to curate for the comparison — that’s what the first chapter purports to do. Robinson and I, African Americans, are age cohorts, both affected to one degree or another by the political world of that era, particularly the one that impacted African Americans. We both graduated from college in spring 1963, went to graduate school at about the same time, reading some of the same literature, receiving our doctorate degrees in political science, and publishing our first books in 1980. Yet I think New Orleans, where I grew up, in all its racial/skin and color/class complexities as I describe, was determinant in my case and so different from the two worlds that formed Robinson, namely Oakland, California, and Alabama, through his family. Oakland, specifically, as my Black relatives who moved there in the early ’50s testified, was quite different from New Orleans regarding the black question. Growing up in the Crescent City taught that the white/black binary was insufficient in making sense of social reality, and that class inequalities figured into the equation. The black world in New Orleans was far bigger and more complex than the one that formed Robinson. It taught me from an early age, therefore, that there was not one such world. The city, in other words, primed me to be open to the intersection of race and class when first presented with the opportunity for investigation. Both Robinson and I visited Africa in our academic preparation. He, basically an undergraduate summertime intern in 1962; I, a graduate student for a year and a half in 1969–1970 to do dissertation research. The two visits, I contend, were more determinant than anything in our political trajectories. The main reason being where we fortuitously went. Robinson to colonial Africa, what was then called Southern Rhodesia, while I had the good fortune to go to Tanzania, almost a decade into independence and the headquarters of the Southern African liberation movements. As I point out in the chapter, I was able to verify with my own eyes what Frantz Fanon’s critique of postcolonial Africa, The Wretched of the Earth — a book that many of us of that generation had dutifully read — argued: namely, the replacement of a European colonial class in Africa with a homegrown one, an emergent bourgeoisie — and with all of the negatives that outcome entailed, ones we tragically live with until today. Fanon’s book, to be noted, figured significantly into the debates between cultural nationalists on one side and revolutionary nationalists on the other side. Bobby Seale, one of the founders of the Black Panther Party, and at the center of the race versus class debate when it first erupted, confirmed in a conversation with me in 1980 that the book was a mandatory reading for the organization — and informed the Black Panther Party’s class-oriented position in the debate. Our two different destinations in Africa were, again, determinant. Robinson could imagine an ideal Africa after independence. Tanzania revealed, at least for me, that independence was insufficient for bringing about social equality in Africa. And if Tanzania seemed to be the best that African independence had to offer, then something more fundamentally radical was needed to achieve that end. That there was a rich debate in Tanzania about that very issue by individuals who impressed me, not the least of whom was Walter Rodney, a neighbor and age cohort, was also my good luck. Thus, why I sometimes say that I went to Africa as a black nationalist/Pan-Africanist and left in search of communism. Perhaps in 1983, when Black Marxism was published, it was too early for Robinson to have an informed opinion about the reality of independence in Zimbabwe. By 2000, however, when the book was republished, he should have known better. His silence then about the tragic situation in Zimbabwe was telling — an inconvenient fact about the “black radical tradition.” Something I didn’t include in my biographical chapter and only thought about later is the vast distance, epistemologically, between Robinson’s and my first book, both published in 1980 — and a reflection of our different African experiences. My Islam and Politics in East Africa: The Sufi Order in Tanzania and his Terms of Order: Political Science and the Myth of Leadership . The two books spoke to our different graduate school training, he largely as a political theorist and I, a comparativist. Terms of Order operates almost exclusively at the level of ideas in books; Islam and Politics is empirically grounded, based on original field research. While the former argues that politics are mainly a Western ordering of the world and absent in traditional African societies, the latter instantiates that politics, the struggle for power, existed in precolonial, colonial, and postcolonial Africa, accompanied by, contra Robinson, leadership. The latter, in fact, was at the very center of my book, namely, how Islam was employed by a religious leader to advance the interests of the formerly enslaved through modern political action. If Robinson were to be believed, the reality I discovered and described was the exception to Africa’s “metaphysical,” as he called it, reality. I contend that what I found and wrote about was more representative of real Africa than Robinson’s mostly classless, apolitical, and ahistorical portrait of Africa. Without going into more detail, suffice it to say that both our books anticipated the very different political trajectories we would take. However influential my background and training might have been in my political direction, I end the chapter with a reminder about luck — good luck specifically — advice all so important for youth today. That’s why I dedicate the book to “the radicalizing youth everywhere in quest of the real Marx.”

articles.title: History From Below: Molly Crabapple’s Here Where We Live Is Our Country
articles.author: DSA Religion and Socialism Working Group
articles.content: There is little new to say about Molly Crabapple’s wonderful history of the Jewish Bund , Here Where We Live is Our Country . Since its publication, the book has been widely celebrated by the Left, dismissed by the Right, and met with a mix of praise and accusations of naivety or idealism from liberal and centrist publications. The praise is well deserved. Crabapple writes so joyfully and tenderly about the Bund that a passive reading of the book feels almost heretical. The Bund was anti-Zionist, and Here Where We Live is Our Country is the kind of book that inspires people to continue the struggle against Zionism and genocide. As I read, I couldn’t help but reflect on what makes good historical writing. I have long held the view that an academic tone and a straightforward, seemingly unbiased telling of history are, frankly, a bad way to write, and an even worse way to engage with historical texts. First, the idea of telling an unbiased history is both naïve and impossible. If one subscribes to the notion that history is a set of facts and that a history book teaches or uncovers those facts, one is doomed to fall into the ruling- class narrative. That narrative promotes a record of great men, civilizations, and empires, in which everyday people are merely passive observers of the ever-turning wheel. Nothing could be further from the truth. Ordinary people are active participants in history, forging the path along which a “great man” or a “grand narrative” of civilization can later be divined. As a counter to the chronicle of great men and grand narratives, a different school of thought has emerged, first articulated by E.P. Thompson in the 1960s as “history from below.” But like most things, “history from below” existed long before Thompson popularized the term. Friedrich Engels ’s The Condition of the Working Class in England , C.L.R. James ’s The Black Jacobins , and Peter Kropotkin’s The Great French Revolution are all excellent examples of history from below before the term was popularized. It was the work of Howard Zinn that breathed new life into the form with his bestseller A People’s History of the United States. These seminal works gave readers a sense of empowerment, showing that working-class people are shaping the world we live in and that, no matter how much the ruling class wishes it were otherwise, history doesn’t just happen to people without their participation. This is where Crabapple’s book really shines. Crabapple weaves the narrative of the Bund with moments from her life as an activist. For Crabapple, the Bund has a personal element. Her great-grandfather, the impressionist painter and sculptor Samuel Rothbort, was a Bundist. It’s through Crabapple’s family lens that we are introduced to the Bundist ideas. This was a movement of Jewish socialists who sought to build autonomy, dignity, and socialism within Europe . Establishing a philosophy of doikayt , Yiddish for “hereness,” Bundists did not believe a Jewish state would bring safety. Bundists saw Zionism as a capitulation to racism and the idea that Jews were foreigners who didn’t belong in Europe.As Crabapple expands the narrative, the reader sees her life as a journalist. We cut between complex historical narratives of the Russian Revolution and the Bundists as well as her time at Occupy Wall Street or her writing on Gaza. The intertwining creates a grand socialist narrative. The Bundists were not naïve, wide-eyed socialists living in a utopian fantasy, as their detractors would describe them. Crabapple lays out the Bundist program with precision and details how Bundists would manage the affairs of cities and town councils. The Bundists did not shy away from power but wielded it within a democratic tradition seeking tangible, day-to-day improvements for the working class. Bundists would put in practice an eight-hour workday in Vilna, Minsk, Grodno, and Białystok long before it became law, secure wage increases for workers, improve safety conditions, and establish mutual aid funds to help injured workers, all while protecting themselves within the framework of “national cultural autonomy.” This was a practical method of Jewish preservation and self-defense that did not rely on “nationalism.” This strategy had practical effects. In the extreme violence of anti-Semitic Tsarist Russia, Bundists were able to defend themselves. The Bund successfully armed self-defense militias and created a Jewish culture of mass resistance. The fact that the Bund could build anything under such harsh conditions is a testament to its practicality. There is much to learn from the Bund and from the Bolshevik response to it. It’s nothing short of a tragedy that the Bolsheviks would go on to reject the Bund and its “national cultural autonomy.” Ultimately, Lenin viewed the Bundists as a separatist threat to the working class. Lenin wanted an organized party of professional revolutionaries while the Bund wanted to remain an autonomous entity within the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party. The Bolshevik reaction to the Bund is a cautionary example. Marginalized groups within the working class can maintain autonomy and apply cultural lenses to address issues affecting those communities. This is not a contradiction to solidarity but an asset to it. The Bund offered a real alternative to Zionism for Jewish people being persecuted in Russia, and support of the Bund within the revolution could very well have solidified Bundism as a viable alternative. That viable alternative feels like a thesis in and of itself. Crabapple continuously invites the reader to imagine a new world. Here Where We Live Is Our Home is a thorn in the side of the ruling order; it is the history of anti-Zionist Jewish thought and movements. For so long, this has been an underarticulated history, known only to those willing to search it out. Now it is available to all of us. Reading it, I felt as if I were reading a first edition of Black Jacobins or The Making of the English Working Class . Like those great works of resistance literature, Crabapple’s book is destined to inspire action. articles.title: Socialists Should Be Champions of Government Efficiency
articles.author: Liza Featherstone
articles.content: Early this week, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, speaking at the Urban 20 (U20) Mayors Summit, bemoaned that government “efficiency has been taken on as a right-wing concern,” with Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) being a particularly vile example. As with the phrase “quality of life,” the mayor observed, “there has been a sense that if you admit to an interest in those things, then you are assisting the Right.”On the contrary, the mayor said: “If you ignore these things,” that’s actually assisting the Right. Government efficiency is “incredibly important,” something “we have to deliver”; he stressed that we can’t let the Right have an “ideological monopoly on it.”The remarks were consistent with a broader effort in the Mamdani administration, which has a charter commission called the Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE), a cheeky reference to Musk’s DOGE. The charter amendments, which will be on the ballot in November, were crafted with consultation — including ten public hearings all over the city — with city workers, small business owners, and other members of the public; they aim to shore up the city’s rainy day fund (its backup savings in case of a crisis) and to lessen red tape in new construction, city procurements, the use of city properties, improvements to street safety, and many other areas.This is a lane that the Left should have long occupied. Government efficiency should be a socialist priority, because socialist governments are asking the public to trust them to do more rather than less. To buy into that project, the public must have confidence that government can deliver and deliver well. Every public dollar wasted on inefficiencies and red tape, or on corrupt middlemen looking to make a buck on the public’s dime, is a dollar that could have gone toward making average people’s lives better and rebuilding people’s trust in government’s ability to act in their interests.Mamdani is not the first socialist mayor to make this case. Bernie Sanders, as mayor of Burlington, Vermont, was successful and popular in part because he balanced budgets and emphasized government efficiency. After Sanders won reelection in 1982, he reflected on his success speaking at a conference in New York City. He noted that many Republicans supported him “because we are now running — as any city government should run — an honest, efficient government,” with centralized purchasing and other sensible reforms.As for COGE, not everyone on the Left has been thrilled with the name, reflecting unease with the project itself. In an online briefing on Tuesday, one question submitted from a member of the public was: Why use the name COGE, given that DOGE has “caused so much harm. People lost their jobs and important services were cut. Is that what COGE is?”“I like this question,” said Susan Kang, a member of the commission and a professor of political science at John Jay College at the City University of New York. She encounters versions of this skepticism a lot. The name, she says, reflects the administration’s belief that “government efficiency is not a right-wing thing. It doesn’t mean a loss of services.” Instead, she said, it should mean “a government that delivers quickly and in a way that uses the labor of city workers well, and that makes our citizens feel heard, respected, and treated in the way they deserve.”Kang also pointed out that the COGE name has succeeded in drawing interest: “If we just called it a ‘charter commission,’” the project would not have made “such a splash. This has become international news.”COGE is part of a series of visible good-government initiatives by this administration. Last spring, Mamdani appointed a chief savings officer to each city agency to identify waste and streamline services and announced reforms to make it easier to deliver affordable housing faster. This summer, he unveiled more than fifty reforms to “slash red tape” for small businesses and created a team of technologists to make city services easier for New Yorkers to access.To execute on more of his agenda, Mamdani will at some point need to ask more of the citizenry. Ray Horton, former president of the Citizens Budget Commission and a retired Columbia Business School professor who has written books about New York City government and its fiscal problems, says demonstrating government efficiency is particularly crucial since Mamdani will need to raise taxes, certainly on the superrich but probably also on single-family homes, which are vastly undertaxed in New York City.If Mamdani “is able to make a case that he is improving the quality of municipal services,” says Horton, a democratic socialist, the argument for higher taxes will be much easier to make.Still, Horton notes that not all the issues addressed by COGE are of earth-shattering importance. He laughingly points out that there is an entire amendment simplifying the permitting for outdoor dining, whereas there are hundreds of pages in the municipal contracts that can complicate the delivery of more crucial services like education. (None of that can be addressed until union contract bargaining next year, a situation that is likely to be fraught as the socialist mayor steps into the role of the boss in bargaining with the unions — a tricky dynamic that has already emerged in his negotiations with the city’s main teachers’ union.)Some of the COGE amendments do touch on big issues like traffic safety. But for those leading this effort, the granularity is also part of the point. As Mamdani put it in his U20 remarks, “The smallest concerns are oftentimes the most important concerns, because that is where you can build those early blocks of trust with a constituent that this government can somehow be different than those which have preceded them.”In contrast to DOGE, which treated government workers as the enemy of the public good, COGE emphasizes that those workers are partners in efficiency, the best experts to guide this process, and stresses how much city workers have to gain from a more functional government.Ann Cheng, executive director of COGE, says she has been drawn to solving these problems partly because she has worked in government in many different capacities; she was a public-school teacher before she went into policy. When you work for the city, Cheng says, you expect the “hard things to be hard, but your easy things are also hard.” Her husband, a teacher, breaks up fights at school — hard work, to be sure — but often gets even more frustrated that it takes six weeks to replace a child’s lost MetroCard.Cheng says city employees understand that it is hard work to dig a water tunnel or plow the city after a snowstorm. But, she asks, “Why is it so hard to get the paperwork signed off?”The charter amendments risk being overlooked, given they aren’t exactly hot-button issues, nor are they overtly ideological. But Kang feels that the Left needs to get more engaged in this fight. Speaking after the briefing Tuesday, in her personal capacity, Kang worried that many on the Left “don’t understand the political importance of the success of these ballot measures.” She hopes that those who support Mamdani’s affordability agenda will grasp the stakes: “The success of these ballot measures,” she says, “is going to be seen as a measure of his ability to be effective in government.” Positioning a left-wing mayor as fiscally responsible, Kang argues, “is an important part of the left governance project.”

articles.title: Amazon Workers Keep Walking Out
articles.content: RIVERSIDE, CALIF. — In February, a worker at Amazon’s DJT 6 delivery station in Riverside was confronted inside the warehouse by a former coworker. She had accused him of harassment. The man had already been fired but somehow got back inside the building. Emmanuel Cadena, who works at DJT 6 and knew the woman, said the man blamed her for his firing. Another worker stepped in. “ He flashed the gun and said, ​ ‘ If you and your friend have a problem, you can see me outside,’” Cadena said. The confrontation happened near the conveyor belt where workers were sorting packages. Amazon did not pause work, according to Cadena. ​ “ There’s no sort of cover in any capacity,” he said. There were no security guards at DJT 6 at the time. Amazon spokesperson Sam Stephenson said, ​ “ The safety of our employees and partners is our highest priority, and we take matters like this incident seriously.” He said Amazon immediately notified local law enforcement and provided resources to employees, and that the company has ​ “ proactively added additional layers of security” at DJT 6 . Workers say that response came only after they pushed for it. They went to management and demanded security guards; Amazon brought in temporary ones, then made them permanent after workers pushed some more. For Cadena, 26 , who has worked at DJT 6 for just over a year, the incident pushed him deeper into an organizing campaign with Teamsters Local 1932 that had gone public in December. Since then, workers have walked out four times, pressed management over safety issues and demanded that Amazon recognize and bargain with their union — which the company has so far refused to do. The Teamsters say a majority of workers at the facility have now signed union authorization cards. On September 2 , workers walked out for the third time since December, this time in a one-day unfair labor practice (ULP) strike over what the Teamsters describe as retaliation against workers advocating for safer working conditions. It was the first time workers on both of DJT 6 ’s primary shifts had walked out together. Cadena got to the station early. Workers on the night shift were already outside picketing. Cadena, who works days, went inside. At 6 : 20 a.m., he and his coworkers gathered near the exit. Management had put three tables together in the break room and covered them with snacks. ​ “ I had never seen so many snacks before since I started working here,” Cadena said. There was more variety than usual, too. ​ “ They could have done this the whole time.” One worker gave a short speech. Cadena estimated that between 50 and 80 workers then walked out together and joined the picket line, where workers carried a banner reading ​ “ FAIR PAY FOR ALL WORKERS” and signs telling Amazon to ​ “ OBEY THE LAW.” Kain Kazsuk, a 27 -year-old night-shift worker who has worked at DJT 6 for nearly two years, has participated in all three walkouts. He joined the organizing effort last August. The campaign went public in December with a walkout during Amazon’s holiday rush. The overnight shift left the building around 1 a.m., and the picket lasted about five hours. Amazon told KVCR that fewer than 1 % of employees at the facility participated. Afterward, Kazsuk said, managers treated some of the most visible organizers differently. ​ “ The day after the walkout, it was almost like we were being shunned,” he said. Eventually, though, ​ “ once they kind of realized that this union thing was not just like a one-time walkout,” Kazsuk said, ​ “ it kind of became more normalized.” Workers have pressed management on other problems, too. Kazsuk said workers concerned about the noise from the conveyor system went to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. Amazon later reworked sections of the conveyor and added sound-dampening material, he said. Workers also began holding what they call ​ “ marches on a manager,” approaching managers in groups on the warehouse floor about problems they want addressed. “ At this point, if there is an issue, we’re going to do something about it,” Kazsuk said. ​ “ We’ve taken back a lot of the power in the warehouse.” In March, workers walked out again after Amazon fired Andres Aguayo, a DJT 6 worker involved in the organizing. Aguayo told KVCR that he and other workers had been approaching supervisors about safety problems and coworkers’ concerns. ​ “ They figured I was enough of a problem that they didn’t want me working,” he said. He said Amazon accused him of misconduct but did not provide evidence. Asked about Aguayo’s firing, Amazon told In These Times , ​ “ Mr. Aguayo was terminated for violating company data policies.” Amazon’s Inland Empire DJT 6 sits in the Inland Empire, the warehouse belt stretching east from Los Angeles through Riverside and San Bernardino counties. Amazon opened its first warehouse there in 2012 . By 2021 , when The New York Times Magazine reported on the company’s growth in the region, it was the Inland Empire’s largest private employer, with 14 facilities, two logistics air hubs and more than 40 , 000 workers. Amazon workers in the region have repeatedly organized over working conditions. During the pandemic, more than 400 workers at the company’s LGB 3 facility in Eastvale signed a petition demanding safer conditions. In August 2022 , workers at the company’s KSBD air hub in San Bernardino walked out over pay and extreme heat. DJT 6 itself has been part of the Teamsters’ Amazon campaign for several years. In October 2023 , unionized delivery drivers from Palmdale brought their picket line there during Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days promotion. The drivers worked for an Amazon Delivery Service Partner; the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) later alleged that Amazon was a joint employer and had unlawfully refused to bargain, among other violations. Two years later, workers employed directly by Amazon inside DJT 6 launched their own public campaign. The Teamsters say a majority of the workforce signed union authorization cards in December, though the union has not petitioned the NLRB for an election. Making Amazon Bargain Near the end of the night shift Wednesday, Kazsuk and another worker tried giving management formal notice of the strike. Managers declined to take the letter, he said, so they left it on a table in the managers’ office. Kazsuk estimated that 45 to 50 night-shift workers left. Some marched up the road with a banner and chants. Others who did not want to be publicly identified simply left. The picket continued into the day shift. “ The trucks stopped,” Kazsuk said. ​ “ The line of cars was not able to move the inventory.” Amazon Flex drivers posted on Reddit that they couldn’t enter the station for scheduled delivery blocks; some said Amazon later notified them they would still be paid. Amazon told The Press-Enterprise that the protest was ​ “ initiated and attended by mostly outside organizers.” Kazsuk rejected Amazon’s characterization. Teamsters organizers had advised the workers, he said, but ​ “ it was all us, boots on the ground in the warehouse, talking to our coworkers.” The day shift had been involved in the organizing before Wednesday, Kazsuk said, but had not previously staged a walkout. He described support as growing ​ “ slowly and steadily” since December. More recently, ​ “ I’ve seen a lot of people who were previously against the whole idea now supporting it.” Asked about the Teamsters’ assertion that a majority of DJT 6 workers had signed union cards, Stephenson said, ​ “ Despite claims to the contrary, the Teamsters don’t represent any Amazon employees or partners, at this site or at any Amazon facility.” Cadena and Kazsuk are directly employed by Amazon. At the company’s JFK 8 warehouse on Staten Island, directly employed workers won an NLRB election in April 2022 . Amazon challenged the result and refused to bargain. This April, the NLRB ruled that Amazon had unlawfully refused to recognize and bargain with the union, which affiliated with the Teamsters in 2024 . Amazon said it would appeal. Four years after the election win, workers still do not have a first contract. At DJT 6 , Kazsuk said the rules of the job can change constantly: Something workers are told to do one day can be prohibited the next and required again the day after that. Cadena sees similar problems on the day shift. He works in OTR, the part of the station that dispatches drivers. He said workers had faulty microphones that required him to take off his work gloves to turn them on and off. Amazon replaced them last month, eleven months after he started. At another point, a shade tent used by workers directing drivers broke. Cadena said a pregnant coworker spent several days working outside in the sun before it was replaced. “ They’re not ever going to admit that the reason that they’re doing it is because we made a fuss about it,” Kazsuk said. “ If we have any more issues, we will definitely make our voices heard,” Cadena said. ​ “ If walking out again is the means necessary to make our voices heard, then we got to do what we got to do.”

articles.title: The Uprising We Got vs. the One We Need
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: How do you make a boring film about a peasant revolt? Writer-director Paul Greengrass ( The Bourne Supremacy , Captain Phillips , United 93 ) has found a way. His new film, The Uprising , is about the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, and it’s such a glum plod I should’ve forgotten it immediately after seeing it. But somehow it haunts me. Maybe it’s the dismal blue-lit cinematography, so typical of our spiritless era. And on top of that, Greengrass’s tendency to favor in intense scenes his wobbling, uncertain handheld-camera work that has so little impact, you want to yell at the screen, “Pick a shot, man! You’re the director!” But mostly, it’s the way the film disapproves of peasant revolts, which you might say is surely impossible. If there’s a peasant revolt, you side with the peasants, obviously — even old Hollywood flicks made by rank conservative movie moguls got that part right. But The Uprising earnestly insists on an “its complicated” stance toward the events of 1381. There’s all that distasteful violence and looting by enraged and starving peasants, for example. And the protagonist, a leader of the massive rebellion, tut-tuts and shakes his head and gets depressed over that in a way that says plainly, “The peasants are revolting in more ways than one.” This view reflects Greengrass’s fundamental take on revolutionary history worldwide throughout recorded time. Once a documentary filmmaker who worked in apartheid South Africa and Northern Ireland, Greengrass maintains his very limited, Cambridge-educated-Brit notion of the breadth of historical events, saying smugly, “Revolutions always eat themselves.” In other words: Why bother? “They start off with people’s intense hopes and dreams, but once you pull authority down, the result is chaos.” Greengrass follows the same logic of Christopher Nolan’s The Dark Knight Rises and many other contemptible movies about the folly of mass revolt, showing that suffering proles driven to the edge by a corrupt ruling class are sympathetic only up until the moment when they rebel and fight back. From then on, unless they repent, they’re the baddies — mindless, bloodthirsty, brutal mobs. They can only become fully sympathetic again in abject defeat — if then. Ploughman, the Worst Superhero Ever The film is not helped along by having our hero played by the stupefyingly dull Andrew Garfield. As the fictional farmer called simply “Ploughman,” he’s in perpetual mourning over his family that died in the black plague. Pushed to his limit by the royal taxes that are beggaring his community, Ploughman assaults the tax-collecting hirelings of King Richard II, thus kicking off the revolt. Ploughman explains that his name refers to the fact that he and his work are regarded as one entity, but hearing it said over and over gets very distracting. What’s with that name anyway? Ploughman . Is he the worst superhero ever? Is his superpower growing potatoes? I should add that Garfield is in no way believable as a fourteenth-century farmer. He has the soft-boy look of some random coffeehouse laptop jockey, yet we’re supposed to accept that he’s a formidable figure, lean and sinewy from a lifetime of hard labor. Wielding his favorite weapon, the sickle — don’t get your hopes up, communists! — he’s such a deadly fighter, he readily defeats the knights who are guarding the king, one after another, in an absolutely delusional action sequence that arrives late in the movie. Honor labor, Greengrass, by acknowledging that a farmer might be very handy with his sickle and still not be able to defeat, on his own, several highly trained knights whose lifelong calling is combat. Unsurprisingly, this lame attempt at an action-oriented historical epic is bombing badly at the box office. It’s the second of two failed films in a row for Garfield after The Magic Faraway Tree , which is the real title of a real movie that opened a few weeks ago and was immediately consigned to oblivion by a disgusted public. Making Ploughman the superhuman Everyman at the center of The Uprising pushes into secondary roles the more interesting historical figures who actually led the revolt, played by more exciting actors — Cosmo Jarvis as renegade soldier Wat Tyler and Jamie Bell as seditious priest John Ball. There was a certain poetry and logic to soldier and priest, sword and scripture, joining forces to lead the most massive peasant revolt in English history. But here, it gets thrown out of whack by shoving a sad-sack farmer into the foreground. Greengrass wants to make sure that women get some screentime too, which is fair enough, so there’s a fictional character named Alyce (Thomasin McKenzie), an ex-nun who was raped by a priest and had her newborn child torn away from her, who’s now a head-shaven toughie ready to fight. And the worried mother of troubled boy king Richard II, Joan of Kent (Katherine Waterston), prays that he’ll find the strength to rule independent of his corrupt and self-serving counselors who include the archbishop of Canterbury, Simon Sudbury (Stephen Dillane), Sir Robert Hales, the grand prior of the Knights Hospitaller (Tom Hollander), and nobleman politician William Walworth (Jonny Lee Miller). Woody Norman as fourteen-year-old Richard II, tormented by nightmares and conniving advisers and presentiments of doom, does a nice job of making the boy king both pitiable and disturbing. He appears to be a weak reed on which to build any confidence, yet the peasants still believe intensely in kings divinely ordained by God and are convinced he’ll cast off his evil counselors once the people petition him with their grievances. When the boy king finally does find the strength to lead, well — I probably don’t have to say “SPOILER ALERT!” when I tell you that this doesn’t go well for the peasants. Or for peasant leaders. Robin Hood and His Morose Men Just to give you one example of what ultimately happened — though it’s not handled this way in the film, which chickens out at every turn — the priest John Ball was executed by being hanged, drawn, and quartered. If you look it up, you’ll find that’s a gruesome multiple-step form of medieval capital punishment that certainly wasn’t the origin of the word “overkill,” but that term comes to mind nevertheless. But that’s a bummer, right? So Paul Greengrass decided to find a way to tack a happier ending onto The Uprising . And this really is a SPOILER: Greengrass has Ploughman escape and then turn up again in an idiotic denouement when the heavily guarded royal coach bearing King Richard II and the Queen Mother is lumbering through the woods and gets surrounded by a bunch of masked figures all wearing dull green who drop down out of the trees. “It’s Robin Hood and his Merry Men,” you think with a sinking sense of despair, and it is, only this bunch is anything but merry. It’s Robin Hood and his Morose Men, starring Ploughman as the beloved masked outlaw of Sherwood Forest, not in the least cheered up by finding this liberating form of ongoing rebellion and guerilla-style warfare. Ex-nun Alyce is now one of the low-spirited gang. Any hopes Greengrass might have cherished that The Uprising would kick off a rebooted Robin Hood series die a well-deserved death right here. Where’s Errol Flynn when you need him? When somebody in The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938) says in shocked tones to Flynn’s Robin Hood, “You speak treason!” he answers with heartening élan, “Fluently.” So goddamn proud of himself and his fellow rebels, I mean. Those were the days. But here, we have the worst of both worlds: gritty “realism” and absurd Hollywood convention. Here Ploughman/Robin Hood has a chance to kill Richard II, this little royal sumb-tch who betrayed Wat Tyler and John Ball and slaughtered thousands of trusting peasants who believed in him. But you can’t count on these dreary depressive half-hearted rebels who never really commit to their own revolution. Ploughman/Robin Hood merely drags the king out of his carriage into the dirt and says scornful words at him. He promises that, after this schoolyard-style humiliation, the boy king will be harassed by a fresh set of nightmares till the end of his days. Yeah, that’s real punishment. An already nightmare-plagued teenage king, safe in his castle, has more nightmares. That’ll show him. How media-makers have embraced utter toothlessness even in fictionalized narratives of historical rebellions is sickening to contemplate. Movies like this are just one more way of reminding ourselves that for decades we’ve been macerating in weak equivocation and class-traitor spinelessness. So there’s yet another promising cinematic premise gone down the chutes — with a bomb this size, nobody will be able to make another 1381 English Peasant Revolt movie for who knows how long. And I’d like to see a unsparingly realistic version of that film that includes some of John Ball’s famous incendiary speeches, such as the one with the mocking kick-ss line, “When Adam delved and Eve span, who then was the gentleman?” Then it should show Ball’s hanged-drawn-and-quartered execution after Richard II reneges on every promise to his too-trusting subjects in order to get them to disband and then hunts down their rebel leaders. Let’s look at this historical uprising squarely. It has, shall we say, enduring relevance.
