articles.title: How Should Socialists Relate to the Market?
articles.author: Vivek Chibber
articles.content: It’s all too common for people to associate the existence of markets with capitalism. But because we know markets had a life before capitalism, we can also imagine them having a life after. On this latest episode of the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism , Vivek Chibber and Melissa Naschek compare how markets operated in precapitalist economies versus modern capitalist economies to see if markets may prove useful in future socialist societies. Confronting Capitalism with Vivek Chibber is produced by Catalyst: A Journal of Theory and Strategy and published by Jacobin . You can listen to the full episode here . Melissa Naschek In our episode on market socialism , you talked about why markets are not inherently capitalist and why the socialist movement should think seriously about how to incorporate them into socialism. Today we’re going to take more of a theoretical and historical approach and look at what markets are, how they operate within capitalism, and why markets could be compatible with a socialist society. Vivek Chibber The neoliberal right and mainstream economics take markets to be synonymous with capitalism. They see capitalism simply as a quantitative expansion of the market. Ironically, there’s a mirror image of this within the Left too. Whenever they see a market, it has to be a capitalist market. And this is where a lot of the objections to market socialism come from. So I think it’s good to see if we can detach markets from capitalism conceptually and then try to show that the market itself is very limited in its properties. How it functions will depend on how it’s embedded in the wider and more encompassing context of other social relations. And that will help us think better about what aspects of the market are intrinsic to it and what aspects of the market actually are ones that are endowed through capitalism. And hence, if we were to take it outside of capitalism, we can see which aspects of markets will remain and which aspects of market will fall away. And it might turn out that the aspects that remain are actually not only unobjectionable but quite useful. Precapitalist Markets Melissa Naschek Why don’t we start, then, with the markets that existed before capitalism. What did markets look like in a precapitalist society? Vivek Chibber In one sense, they looked like markets do anywhere else, which is to say that they were places where people went to buy and sell stuff. But in a deeper sense, the markets were very different prior to the rise of capitalism . Before capitalism, the buying and selling of things occupied a much more peripheral and marginal place in economic activity. The actual existence of trade is thousands of years old. It’s existed almost since the deepening of settled agriculture. But it’s also known that the trade tended to be of goods that were what you might call “surplus production.” Prior to the rise of capitalism, the fundamental production unit was the peasant family farm. And the peasant farm overwhelmingly raised crops and made things for its own consumption. This sometimes was taken to be a sign of what’s called a natural economy. Within a natural economy, every unit was taken to be totally self-sufficient. They produced just for themselves, and nobody traded. But we now know that has never been the case. Natural economies are mostly fictional entities. Even when people were primarily growing and making things for themselves, they always engaged in trade. But the trade they engaged in tended to be of stuff that was left over after their consumption needs were taken care of. They took those to the market. And most markets tended to be rural or village markets. They didn’t go to the cities. Melissa Naschek When you say consumption needs, can you just clarify that? Vivek Chibber The peasant family primarily engaged in agriculture. It would grow crops. Depending on the country, some of this would be a grain like wheat or rice. And then there would also be other subsidiary crops that they grew on the side, many of which were used for fertilizer. So you would consume some of it, and then the rest, like turnips, you would use for fertilizer. The family unit also made its own manufactured goods. So prior to the rise of capitalism, manufacture and agriculture were not separated as economic activities. The same unit that did agriculture also did manufacture. And Karl Marx speaks eloquently in Capital about how, with the rise of capitalism, you get a division of labor in which, for the first time, manufacturing activity and agricultural activity become functionally separated from each other. Manufacturing is done in urban areas or in different localities, and agriculture is done as a separate activity. Melissa Naschek So in theory, the rural peasant family is self-sustaining just by its own production? Vivek Chibber Let’s say it strives toward self-sufficiency, never achieving it. Melissa Naschek Right, because then you mentioned that there are subsidiary things that they were going to market for. Vivek Chibber Exactly. They would grow their own crops, but then they would also try to build some of their own tools. They would also try to make their own clothes. They would, to the extent that they could, make whatever furniture is possible. But obviously they couldn’t do all of these things. Some of it they would have to get from elsewhere, either from, say, blacksmiths or carpenters within their village. And in India, you had something called the Jajmani system. The Jajmani system was one in which different groups of people specialized in particular things that they made and were usually organized around caste. And then they would exchange with each other through that specialization, but in a non-monetized way. It would be exchange in kind. This many shoes for this many shirts, that kind of thing. Melissa Naschek Would you still consider that a market? Vivek Chibber It’s not a market. It’s exchange activity. We call a market something where there is a concentration of exchange in a specialized location. So suppose different families are trading with each other in the same village. It’s not a market. But now suppose you put a place separately where everybody brings their wares when they want to put them up for sale or trade with somebody. Now you’ve got a market. But before the rise of capitalism, there weren’t a lot of markets in that sense. Most exchange took place informally and locally. So first, not much of the product was actually put up for exchange. What was put up for exchange was stuff left over from the family’s primary production; those things were taken to the market. This means that the production activities were not done with trade in mind. The implication is that peasant producers didn’t care so much about cost and quality. I made it for myself to my liking, and I made it at a cost that I don’t really worry about being competitive, since that’s an afterthought for me. But that means that the stuff that’s coming to the market is neither very cheap nor very good. It’s just stuff that is there, and if you want to buy it, you can buy it. Now, what about the cities? Interestingly, the cities, right up until the fifteenth century or so, were of two kinds: large urban cities and the smaller townships. Most urban settlements were small townships before the rise of capitalism, and these townships are actually an extension of the rural areas. They are not, as Max Weber thought, islands of urban activity and mercantile activity separate from, say, the feudal economy. Cities were actually controlled by feudal lords. Melissa Naschek What is their role in the feudal society in that case? Vivek Chibber Both consumption and production. There were places where feudal lords took some of the stuff that they were having made, but they were also mainly places where people, if they moved out of the village, would come and live, and then they would engage in some kind of mercantile activity. But that mercantile activity was controlled by guilds, and guilds were essentially urban merchant associations or producer associations — carpenters, tradesmen, things like that. And those guilds tightly controlled the markets. So it’s not the case that there was a flourishing market in urban areas that would then spread into the rural areas, like capitalism spreading from the city to the rural areas. The cities were completely controlled by feudal lords. Their economies were run and controlled by the guilds, and the guilds could only control the urban economy if landlords gave them monopoly powers. The cities could not, therefore, be a source of opposition to feudal lords in the way that Weber thought. Cities were in fact primarily and overwhelmingly controlled and dependent upon feudal lords. Markets, therefore, were not a dissolving element to feudalism anywhere in the world. They were internal to feudalism. And what that tells us is markets are not a solvent. Wherever you put them, they don’t just spread like a virus across the economic activity. They are as much under the influence and control of political relations as anything else is. So prior to the rise of capitalism, markets were fully contained, they were limited in what they could do, and they were limited in their impact upon society. But that also means that finding a market prior to the modern era is not evidence that capitalism was coming about or was on its way, because that relies on the assumption that prior to capitalism, there was a natural economy in which there were no markets. That’s wrong. It also relies on the assumption that once you have a market, it has this internal engine that causes it to spread everywhere. That’s not the case. They were limited and contained as long as the class structure and the production relations remained feudal. Melissa Naschek The theorists who have argued that capitalism has been steadily developing since the beginning of human civilization have pointed to markets as part of their proof. And what you’re saying here is that capitalism is not just some natural outgrowth of economic relations and exchange but in fact an imposed and discrete political-economic system. Vivek Chibber That’s exactly right. Capitalism cannot be understood as simply the result of the natural growth of the market, because — this is the important thing — the market did not grow naturally. It existed, but it actually ebbed and flowed. From about the year 1000 CE to 1350 CE, it grows, but then it recedes for about eighty to a hundred years. Then it starts growing again. From thirty thousand feet on high, you can say, “Okay, if you just look at history long enough, you can see that there’s been a growth of the market.” But that misses the fact that for the market to have grown, it required prior political changes first. There was nothing natural about the growth of the market and, therefore, nothing natural about the rise of capitalism. When capitalism does come about, it’s because there is a discrete and very specific change in class relations from lord and peasant to capitalist landlord and tenant farmer, then later capitalist and worker. And that took very specific actions. It’s conceivable that it might not have happened for several more centuries. Capitalist Markets Melissa Naschek So how did capitalism transform markets? Vivek Chibber This is the really important thing. As I said, prior to the rise of capitalism, market exchange existed. Markets as discrete places in society existed. But the things being traded were things that are surplus, that are left over after you’ve made your stuff. And the things being traded were never made with the intent of selling them. And so they weren’t disciplined in the producer’s mind right from the start with the intention that this commodity has to be good enough to sell, cheap enough to sell, and have a market available. He just made them for himself. The second thing is that because they were peripheral and marginal, they never really controlled people’s lives. People’s lives were overwhelmingly determined by their own production units — their own consumption habits and consumption needs, by the growing and the creation of stuff for themselves — and by the authority relations around them, which were aristocrats, feudal lords, or, if it’s Rome, maybe slaveholders. But markets did not have much of an impact on people’s lives. People didn’t depend on them for their livelihood. They didn’t depend on markets for their consumption goods. What changed with capitalism is not just that the market became bigger, more expansive, and consistently growing — although of course that’s true. What changed is that, for the first time, market exchange comes to rule people’s lives in a very fundamental way. The deepest way in which it rules their lives is this. Before the rise of capitalism, what was a basic production unit? As I said, it’s the family farm, the peasant unit. And within that unit, people grow stuff for themselves and rely on their own labor, which is unpaid. They’re working for themselves. When capitalism comes about, what’s the basic production unit? Let’s just say stylistically, it’s the factory. And in that unit, what is the typical form of labor now? It’s wage labor. Now of course, wage labor can be found in all sorts of precapitalist societies. It existed, but it was small in the proportion of the labor force that actually engaged in it. And the people who did wage labor often did it as a “side hustle” — they didn’t depend on it. Now, what’s the defining element of capitalism? People no longer have their own plots of land. They were kicked off the land, which is called expropriation. Peasants became workers. And with that, they had no choice but to sell their labor-power in order to get the money to make the goods. Previously they grew their own goods. Now they have to buy them. Melissa Naschek Some of what you’re saying is that, even though capitalism didn’t invent the labor market, the role that the labor market comes to play under a capitalist society has qualitatively changed. Vivek Chibber Exactly. Not just quantitatively but also qualitatively changed. It’s possible to have a quantitative expansion of the labor market without it changing its quality. This could involve more peasants doing their side hustles, resulting in the labor market growing, or the wage-labor market growing, but it wouldn’t change in its actual functions in society. Melissa Naschek Just like in our day-to-day, when the labor market expands or contracts, it doesn’t signal some kind of major shift within the structures of capitalism. Vivek Chibber Yes, that’s just a quantitative expansion or contraction of an institution, but the role of that institution hasn’t changed. What happened with the rise of capitalism is, for the first time ever, people had to buy the stuff they need to survive, and in order to buy the stuff, they need money. And since money doesn’t grow on trees, the only way they can acquire it is by selling something. The thing they sell is their labor-power. So capitalism is a system in which everybody sells in order to buy. Everybody’s selling something. Capitalists sell goods and services. Workers sell their labor-power. They become dependent on the labor market in a way that no peasant ever was. And the reason that mattered for the peasant was, if, say, there were no jobs in the urban area or nearby villages, the peasant would still be okay, because they had their plot of land. They would still survive. The farm was essentially their social insurance. With the wage-labor market, you become completely dependent on the market for your survival. That puts you at the mercy of two things. First of all, it puts you at the mercy of the guy giving you the job, because if he fires you, you’re out on your butt, and you’re not going to survive. Secondly, the wage-labor market makes you dependent on money and having enough to be able to survive. Money within capitalism became a central social institution in a way that it never was before. So capitalism universalized and expanded two markets. A market for labor, which had never occupied a central place in society. And the other is a market for products. In the past, people took a surplus to the market, stuff that was left over after their consumption needs. They never made things specifically with selling in mind. Now with capitalism, the capitalists who own the factories can’t consume the stuff they’re making, because a lot of the stuff they’re making is things like metal goods. You can’t consume it. The only reason you’re interested in making it is that it’ll get you money. Melissa Naschek Can you talk about the relationship between production and exchange within a capitalist system? Vivek Chibber Prior to the rise of capitalism, exchange had no deep connection to production. Production was carried out for use, for your own consumption. Exchange occurred as a side activity, and often peasant households would do very little exchange. And as I said, the result of that was that the products that were taken to the market were of uneven quality, oftentimes not cost-efficient, not that concerned with whether there is a market for them. Within capitalism, every capitalist knows that unless the products he makes sell in sufficient quantity and at a sufficient profit in the market, he’s going to lose his assets or his factory, et cetera. So right from the start, the capitalist has to make things that are cost-efficient and that are of good quality. Now, you might ask, “So what?” Melissa Naschek Right, this feels very commonsensical to us because we’re living in a capitalist system. Vivek Chibber But there’s a political and social consequence of this. Because every capitalist has to fundamentally be concerned with things like cost-effectiveness, unit costs, and quality, he has to worry about how the work that people are doing for him is being carried out. The capitalist brings labor into the workplace. He could say to the workers, “Hey man, look, I’ve hired you for eight hours. I’m going leave now and I’ll be back at five o’clock. Whatever you’ve made, just hand it over to me and I’ll go sell it.” Melissa Naschek Wow, sounds like a great boss. Vivek Chibber Yeah, that’s the kind of boss everyone wants. But nobody has that boss. Why? Because the capitalist knows, if I commit to paying this person, I have to have revenues from my sales that are high enough to pay for this person and to have my profits. And those revenues are not going to come easily, because there’s somebody else competing with me on the market to sell the same things that I’m selling . So that means if he’s going to survive, he has to be concerned with cost-effectiveness and quality from top to bottom in all of his operations. But that means he cannot trust his workers. He cannot trust them to provide labor in the quantity and of the quality that he wants. And that means that he has to exert power over them and make them work faster, harder, and better. And that puts him at loggerheads with the workers. See what’s happening? This is creating the basis for class struggle. If capitalists didn’t care about the quality and the quantity of their goods, they’d let workers do whatever they wanted. And if they did that, there would never be conflict between these two classes. Why do they care so much? It’s because production is right from the start shaped by exchange. That was not true before the advent of capitalism. What happens in capitalism is exchange on the market takes over your life. It takes over your life directly if you’re a wage laborer, in that you’ve got to go sell your laboring activity on the market. It takes over directly for the capitalist because he has to make sure that whatever goods are being made under his authority are sellable, are good enough. And then indirectly, it is the institution, the factor that creates the conflict between labor and capital, because if the capitalist is going to survive, he’s got to make his profits. If he’s going to make his profits, he’s got to sweat the worker’s labor. If he’s going to sweat the worker’s labor, there’s going to be a conflict. The capitalist market fundamentally changes all social relations because, once you have people dependent on the market, everything else changes around them. Their culture is going to change. How they think about the world is going to change. The social institutions they make are going to change. Everything changes. And that’s why Marx thought that until you dramatically reduce the place of the market or roll it back altogether, you’re not going to be able to bring about the kind of social changes that we would associate with a more humane and just society. Melissa Naschek Speaking of Marx, I wanted to ask: How did he understand markets, and how does a Marxist understanding of the economy differ from that of conservative economists? Vivek Chibber Marx’s theorization of the market is the most profound analysis of market activity that social science has ever come up with. And it’s something of an achievement of modern social science that it manages to marginalize and ignore Marx on this issue. It takes real dedication to marginalize such a profoundly insightful theory. But universities have managed to do that. There is a deep difference between Marx’s view of the market and the conservative one. The conservative view of the market sees it fundamentally as an arena of opportunity and freedom . How? Well, for the conservatives, there are no power relations involved in the market. You go to the market, you bring your stuff along, and either somebody’s going to buy it or not. Nobody’s forcing anyone to buy anything. Nobody’s forcing anyone to sell anything. And if you find that your stuff is not selling, you’ll go back home and you’ll make something else. And you bring that. The beauty of the market is that, through an iterative process, sellers find out what society wants. Because if some stuff doesn’t sell, it means no one wants it. If the stuff does sell, it means it’s meeting a need. And then because all the sellers want to make a profit, they keep looking for things that will sell. And through that process, they end up making things that are actually desired and actually needed. From the buyer’s standpoint, they go to the market knowing exactly what they want. And if what they want isn’t there, they let it be known that, “Hey, we’d really like to have some shoes. There are no shoes here.” And somebody will make shoes for them because it’s a market waiting to be tapped, as they say. So there’s this iterative process from both sides. And everybody gains. Everybody’s happy. Nobody can force any one thing on the other. That’s the conservative side, including the labor market. From the conservative standpoint, labor markets are as much a realm of freedom as product markets. Why? Because if I come to work for you, and I don’t like the way you’re treating me, I can just quit and go work for somebody else. Nobody’s forcing me. I’m not a serf. I’m not a slave. I can quit and go work for somebody else. And that’ll be punishment to you as a bad employer. You’ll have to change your ways. Vice versa, if you hire me and you don’t like the work I’m doing, you can get rid of me. You can fire me, and you’ll hire somebody else. In these fully free exchanges, each person has an exit option. And it’s exactly like when you go to a stall in a flea market. If you don’t like what you’re getting, you go to the next stall. If a capitalist doesn’t like the work that the worker is doing, he’ll go to the next worker. If the worker doesn’t like the way his employer is behaving, he’ll go to the next employer. No coercion, all voluntary action, and it’s a realm of freedom. As Paul Samuelson famously said, employees hire their employers as much as the employers hire them. Melissa Naschek Sounds nice. Vivek Chibber It does sound nice. The thing is, it’s based on a completely hallucinatory understanding of how labor markets actually work. But before I explain that, let me say, it’s not that the entire description is wrong. There is an aspect of the market, especially the product market — the market for goods and services — that is really free and expansive. And Marx admired that. He understood that. Melissa Naschek Right, as much as we talk about exploitation, we’re not saying that wage labor and slavery are comparable institutions. Vivek Chibber Exactly. The fact that I can quit my job, go to somebody else, is a massive advance over being enslaved or over being somebody’s serf. That’s real. That said, there is a genuinely fictional component of the conservative description. It is true to say that I can quit my job working for you and go work for somebody else. But it does not follow from that that there are no power relations between us. Actually, Adam Smith had the best explanation for this, and Smith is known as the founding father of modern economics and a trailblazer for defending capitalism. In fact, Smith hated capitalism — he just said that it was better than the alternative at the time, which was feudalism, and he admired its efficiency gains. Smith said that anytime there is a standoff between an employer and an employee, it’s pretty clear who’s going to win: the employer wins every time. And the reason the employer wins is that he has so much more wealth at his disposal that if his workers refuse to work for him, he can just rely on his stocks of wealth. Back then, it was his inventories, his corn, whatever he had in his granary. But today we would say it’s his assets, it’s his stock portfolio, his savings. Whereas workers have no savings, and if they do, it’s usually only enough to tide them over for a week, two weeks, or a month. In that situation, the employer is always going to win precisely because of his greater wealth and assets. He can hold off longer. So the mere fact that I can change my employment venue from you to somebody else doesn’t mean that the power that the two of you have over me disappears. All it means is I’m going from one situation in which I’m the inferior party to another situation in which I’m again the inferior party. What might change is the degree to which I am mistreated by one or the other, or the degree to which I’m vulnerable to you or the other. But the vulnerability itself never goes away. This means that the labor market is intrinsically and inalterably a site of domination. It’s a site where power is wielded by one party over the other regardless of what the rate of unemployment is. In mainstream economics, if every worker has a job, it equalizes the bargaining relationship. But it never really does, precisely because even if everyone has a job, and they’re able to raise their wages, they never equalize the power relation between themselves and their employers. And that’s why Marx thought the only way to actually democratize economic relations is by eliminating the workers’ dependence on finding an employer for themselves. Melissa Naschek So would it be fair to say that Marx’s critique is centered on the labor market? What about nonlabor commodities? Vivek Chibber The pillar on which the moral critique of capitalism rests for Marx is exploitation. And exploitation occurs between labor and the employer. So you could say that the labor market is the foundation, is the central institution, that Marx is aiming at when he criticizes capitalism. But of course it’s not the only one. Marx also thinks that there’s something about the human beings relating to each other through things, through the commodity, through buying and selling, through only meeting each other in a very instrumental way as sellers and buyers of commodities, that’s also, he thinks, dehumanizing. We abstract away from our personhood, from our individuality. And that means that the richness of potential sociability between us is now set aside in favor of this very crass instrumental need. And for Marx that’s a dimension of what he calls alienation . Then there’s also the problem of the immorality of my having to rely on the market for my basic necessities. Imagine if there’s no wage labor at all. I’m given some kind of basic minimum support, but I still need to find all the stuff I need on the market. And there’s no guarantee that it’s going to be made. To give you a great example, suppose it’s decided by the people who control markets that certain pharmaceuticals are just not profitable enough for them, and they’re not going to make them. Even though wage labor has been abolished, the production of goods is still completely dependent on profitability and whether or not those goods bring adequate profits to the person, instead of being ruled by people’s needs. Marx also objected to that. I think it’s true that most of Marx’s moral and political theory revolves around the extraction of work, the consequences of that, both at the micro level and the macro level. But he thinks there are aspects of markets and market dependence writ large that also have evils of their own. And that’s why, in his mind, it really was an imperative to reduce or abolish the market altogether. Melissa Naschek So let’s keep talking about exploitation. What role does the market play in capitalists exploiting their workers? Vivek Chibber People normally think of exploitation in a very commonsensical way, as when you’re really treating somebody badly. In Marx’s economics, there is a dimension of that in exploitation. That’s why he calls it exploitation. In Marx’s view, when workers are being exploited, they are being treated badly in some way. But it’s not just like they are pushed around or being dominated. For him, it’s something quite specific in addition to the fact that they’re dominated — because they are dominated. Workers are exploited because they end up providing capitalists their labor in such a quantity that capitalists don’t have to work anymore. Capitalists derive their income and livelihood from the work done by workers. What does that mean? It means that you come and work for me and you make stuff. And when I sell the stuff, the revenues from it are enough to both feed you and to give me an income, regardless of whether or not I’ve worked. So in mainstream economics, they’ll often say, ‘Well, the capitalists’ profits are just his wages. They’re wages from the fact that he also contributes to production. He manages, he supervises, he thinks hard. . . . ” Okay, you can say that. But here’s the difference. If a worker isn’t working, he doesn’t get a wage. That’s simple enough. If a capitalist decides not to work, he can still claim his profit, because his profits were never based on the fact that he’s working. They were based on the fact that he owns the factory. If he does work alongside the worker, whether it’s management or anything else, that’s just something he decided to do. He could just as well hire somebody else to do it and pay them. Capitalist income is always a claim on property. Workers’ income flows from their actual laboring activity. And the test is: if workers stop working, they starve. If the capitalist stops working, he just sits around all day, and the income still keeps coming in. That’s exploitation. The exploitation is the extraction of labor. You work for me, and you work long and hard enough that your labor actually provides an income for both of us. The question is: Why do capitalists do it? The answer is simple. If they don’t do it, their operations go under. So if I hire people to work for me, but I do not extract labor from them — what’s called a surplus — then I don’t have the profits and the revenues to plow back into the factory as reinvestment, nor do I have enough for me to live on. I can pinch pennies on my end. But at the end of the day, if you are not making enough stuff for me with an efficiency and of the quality that I need, that I can sell at a profit, my factory will go under. And that means if I want to succeed, I’ve got to get you to make stuff for me that is cheap, that is competitive, and that customers will buy. That requires that I supervise you; that I make sure you work really hard as fast as possible; not just fast enough, not just well enough, but at the highest possible level, because that’s how I beat my competitors. It’s because I’m obsessing over my competitors that I treat you the way I do. Because otherwise, I could just leave, come back at five and say, “Hey Melissa, I’ll see you in eight hours. Work if you want, work if you don’t want, but at the end of the day, as long as there’s enough for us to live on, we’ll be happy.” Why does no capitalist do that? It’s because they’re competing with each other. It’s because they have to get not just some labor out of their employees but the maximum labor out of their employees. Markets force them to do it, which again brings Marx back to saying, “Don’t tell capitalists to be better people. Don’t tell them to behave better; they’re not behaving the way they are because of their personalities. They’re behaving the way they are because the pressure is on them to make a profit.” And so if you want better employers, if you want a society in which the work relation itself is more humane, you’ve got to eliminate the pressure of profit maximization, that pressure of constantly extracting more labor, and that comes from the capitalist market. Postcapitalist Markets Melissa Naschek If markets are playing this huge role in exploitation and essentially forcing the owners of industry to exploit their workforce, how can we think that markets would be a neutral or even good thing under socialism? Vivek Chibber That’s a very good question. And indeed, the onus is on market socialists like myself to justify having markets. Just as I said, I laid the gauntlet down to people who support planning to say they need to make an argument for why they think planning could work when it never actually has anywhere else . So I think the justification for markets is twofold. One is that if it is indeed correct that central planning is a nonstarter, then it’s just a matter of necessity. You’re going to have to have markets to a greater or lesser extent whether you like it or not, because the alternative, which is a fully planned economy, is not a workable alternative. Now, that’s just a recognition of reality. And so a lot of socialists treat the issue of markets and planning as if they’re items on a menu. How can you say you don’t want central planning ? It assumes a choice where there might not be one. And it’d be really, really great if people on the Left could just be pragmatic about this and realize that you cannot treat this as if it’s just all up to you, whether you can opt for door number one, which is markets, or door number two, which is planning. I think it’s perfectly fine to say we would prefer to have planning, and then ask: Could we actually have it? And that’s a great way to then say, “Okay, let’s plan those things that can be planned. And if we find that there’s things that are not amenable to it, then we accept the market in those domains, but, most importantly, we have to then neutralize those components, those aspects of the market that are obnoxious, that generate all these bad outcomes morally, politically, economically inside capitalism.” Melissa Naschek I took from what you said on market socialism that it’s also not quite an either-or; that markets are in fact a tool that can be used, if not fully to plan an economy, then to facilitate a more planned economy compared to what we have now. Vivek Chibber Yeah, compared to what we have now — because in a market socialist economy, there will be more planning than there is in a capitalist economy. I don’t know if I put it as they facilitate planning. What they do is they complement planning. So one part of the economy is planned — and I said this would be things like transportation, utilities, media, and medical care. These are easy to plan because they’re substantially planned even inside capitalism. But when it comes to a lot of consumption goods, like services, like restaurants and hotels and small operations, like sporting goods stores and things like that, I just don’t see how you’ll ever be able to plan those. The goal, then, is that you have those things be put up in the market, but the employment relation and the ownership relations within them have to be different than they are in capitalism. So perhaps you can have enterprises producing goods for the market, but they’re all going to be co-ops. There won’t be an owner inside them. They’ll be paying their workers wages, but the wage will have a fixed component to it, where every enterprise has to give their workers something like a living wage, no matter what. And then on top of the living wage, the co-op can decide, if it wants to take some of its revenues and distribute them as wages, or if it want to take its revenues and perhaps put them in investment or something like that. The key thing is that there will be no owning class. If there’s no owning class, then all the key decisions about how fast to work, when to work, what to make, they’re all made democratically by the workers themselves. The enterprises will compete with each other. Now, won’t competition force them to do the same things that competition forces owners to do in capitalism? No, because your entire fate is not bound up with the success of your enterprise. So in market socialism, people who are working in the market sector would get a nominal wage, but they would also get a huge social wage. That is, guaranteed access to goods like housing, health care, childcare. All of these sorts of things will be citizenship rights. That means, then, that when you’re making your decisions in your co-op about how to distribute your revenues and how to use them, you won’t be burdened with this idea that unless you put all of that stuff back into investment, so that you can drive down the cost of your goods, you’re going to be out on your butt without any kind of survival chances. Because even if your enterprise goes under, you will still have access to certain basic goods as a citizenship right. That means competition won’t exert the same force on you that it does in capitalism. These are just ideas, and I think we have to think through them further. The reason I’m very serious about it is that you can’t just wave your hand and say we’re going to have central planning. Either it works or it doesn’t. And not to have discussions of a fallback option like market socialism is just irresponsible. Because if you take this leap in the dark again at a fully planned economy and it fails again, the result of it is not neutral. People will turn against not just planning, but the whole socialist idea itself. And they’ll say, “Screw it, let’s go back to capitalism.” And you’ll have a movement backward, a new constitution, new rules, new laws, and you’ll bring back capitalism because at least it works. I would just tell socialists: Don’t make the same mistake that mainstream economists do, which is that whenever they see a market, they think it’s capitalism in germinal form. Markets, depending on the wider context, just do different things. It’s still called a market because it has a thin veneer that is common across different systems. But if you just look vertically and how it’s embedded in those systems, it’s those vertical ties to the deeper system that really give it whatever functions it has. What that means then is: Don’t think that if we have markets in socialism, we’re bringing in capitalism. That’s just not true.

articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: DSA chapters across the golden state from San Diego to Humboldt have endorsed candidates and ballot measures and are mobilizing to support them. Here our contributors lay out what we are up to in promoting a democratic socialist political agenda. Santa Barbara DSA Santa Barbara has decided to endorse candidates for local city council, including a mayoral candidate. As of 2024, Santa Barbara has enjoyed a slight 4-3 progressive majority on City Council, allowing for such policies as a local Rent Stabilization Ordinance and the non-renewal of a contract with Flock. However, this majority hangs in the balance in the upcoming election with four seats on council being up for grabs. The current mayor, a conservative man who has hurt progress in the city, has decided not to run for reelection, and three council members have termed out, two of whom are progressives. One of these progressive city council members, Kristen Sneddon, has decided to run for mayor and has received our endorsement due to her continued work on protecting renters and her overall alignment with DSA principles. We have also endorsed Gabe Escobedo, Ian Baucke, and Devon Wardlow, who are running for the other City Council seats in different districts. All of them have shown willingness, if not eagerness, to work with our local chapter. Furthermore, they all support strong tenant protections and are adamant on limiting ICE activity in Santa Barbara to whatever extent they are able. DSA-SB is incredibly focused on the local level and therefore has made no other endorsements. —Beckett S Los Angeles We’re excited to announce the results of our phase 3 electoral endorsement process! DSA-LA is proud to newly endorse: Nithya Raman for Los Angeles City Mayor Angela Gonzales-Torres for Congressional District 34 Noland Sutherland for Burbank City Council Mike Van Gorder for Burbank City Council Stephan Post for West Hollywood City Council Estefany Castenada for Centinela Valley UHSD Trustee Yaritza Gonzalez for Inglewood Unified School District, Trustee They join their fellow members Marissa Roy and Estuardo Mazariegos on our team of union leaders, renters, tenant organizers, parents, and activists who are running for office to fight for working class values and create real change across Los Angeles. You can learn more about our candidates on our website shakeup.la . DSA-LA is ready to unite tenants, union members, immigrant communities, and working Angelenos behind a slate that can break corporate interests’ grip on city government. Our vision is clear: win office, build a governing majority, and deliver a city working people can afford to call home. But we can’t win without your help: now’s the time to mobilize to knock doors, organize your neighbors, and get out the vote. San Diego DSA San Diego canvasses for Alexander Kraft for mayor. This November, DSA San Diego has endorsed two mayoral candidates and two ballot measures. Kenneth Zuniga is a longtime DSA member running for Mayor of the city of Vista here in San Diego County! He served on the Homelessness Commission and has successfully organized to keep ICE out of city facilities. He has also organized against the installation of Flock cameras in Vista. As Mayor, he hopes to lower the cost of living in the city, and advocate for union-backed jobs and truly affordable housing. Alexander Kraft is a socialist labor organizer running for Mayor of El Cajon. Kraft is fighting back against the far-right mayor and city council, for police reform, housing, and protecting El Cajon’s large immigrant community from ICE. The chapter has also endorsed two ballot measures aimed at funding important services through taxing the rich. These measures are Proposition 40 and Proposition 3. Prop 40 is a one-time 5% emergency wealth tax on billionaires in the state, raising 100 billion dollars to fund healthcare and education. This measure was created after Medicaid funds were taken away from Californians by the federal government (called “Medi-Cal” in California). It is vital that this passes so that millions of working-class people don't lose their healthcare. Prop 3 is a proposal to make permanent an existing tax on high-income earners to help fund K-12 and community college education. The loss of this funding would be incredibly detrimental to the future of access to education. DSA San Diego is excited to support these campaigns and continue building socialism in the region! Orange County Over the past few months, OC DSA has seen an undeniable socialist surge to over 800 dues-paying members in good standing. articles.title: Tax California Billionaires Now!
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: [reprinted by permission from The Press Democrat ] This Labor Day (weekend), it’s essential to highlight that reducing inequality is the main purpose of labor unions through collective bargaining for living wages, comprehensive benefits, and improved workplace health and safety conditions. Moreover, unions provide a political voice for their members and lobby for legislation, such as restrictions on child labor, a minimum wage, the forty-hour week, and Social Security, that benefit all working people. Recently, the California Federation of Labor Unions, representing 1300 affiliated unions with 2.3 million members, endorsed Proposition 40, the California Billionaire Tax Act on the November ballot. Prop 40 is a one-time 5% wealth tax spread over five years on California’s 250 billionaires who lived here on January 1, 2026. Prop 40 defines wealth as the value of stocks, bonds, trusts, and specified property holdings, minus outstanding debt. According to the California Budget and Policy Project, if approved, Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg’s net worth would decline from $200 billion to $190 billion. Why is such a tax necessary? First, wealth inequality has soared nationally and in California. A report by UC Berkeley economists Gabriel Zucman and Emmanuel Saez, and Jasper Boll of the Paris School of Economics, finds that from 1982 to 2026, California billionaires' wealth has skyrocketed by 38-fold to $2.3 trillion, while the real family income of the average California family has merely doubled. Second, the measure would generate about $100 billion in revenue that the state desperately needs because of the massive Trump tax cuts for the wealthy last year and the slashing of health care funding (H.R. 1). The Kaiser Family Foundation estimates that up to 1.6 million California Medi-Cal recipients could lose health insurance. Eighty-three California hospitals are at risk of closing, and up to 145,000 health care workers could be laid off, according to the UC Berkeley Labor Center. Ninety percent of the Prop 40 revenue will backfill these health care cuts, with the balance dedicated to public education. Third, Zucman, Saez, and Boll claim that billionaires pay less in taxes than the average taxpayer, relative to income. They calculate that between 2018 and 2020, across all local, state, and federal taxes, billionaires paid just 24 percent of their income in taxes, whereas the typical taxpayer paid 30 percent. The main reason is that both the federal government and California tax investment income or capital gains (about 72 percent of billionaire wealth) only when stock is sold. Most billionaires earn very little in salaries, such as Zuckerberg’s, which is $1 a year. They borrow tax-free against their colossal wealth to pay for ongoing expenses. The billionaire tax provides a remedy by taxing all wealth regardless of whether it has been realized or not. The argument opponents make is that if Prop 40 passes, billionaires will leave the state, resulting in the loss of capital and jobs. However, there is no historical evidence to support this assertion. Sociologist Cristobal Young, author of The Myth of Millionaire Tax Flight (2017), studied 13 years of millionaire tax records nationwide and found that only 2.4 percent of millionaires moved to another state annually, compared with 2.9 percent of the population at large. Young also researched California millionaires after the voters in 2012 approved the largest tax increase ever on top earners. Two years after the ballot initiative, the state experienced a loss of just .04 percent of millionaire residents. Studies reached similar conclusions for other states boosting taxes on the wealthiest, including New Jersey in 2020, New York in 2021, and Massachusetts in 2022 Why? The research has found that 60 percent of California millionaires are older than 50 years; most have children and are socially and professionally tied to where they made their money. With children in school, property ownership, and extensive professional and social connections, they are unlikely to move for tax reasons. Moreover, California tech billionaires depend on skilled professionals who are graduates of UC and CSU, and on innovation that is a byproduct of the exchange of ideas among tech workers across companies clustered in places like Silicon Valley and San Francisco. California billionaires benefit immensely from the publicly financed infrastructure of universities, transportation, and healthcare. It’s time for them to pay their fair share to offset the pending catastrophic health care cuts.

articles.title: NONONO on Propositions 41, 42, 43
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Most of the attention on the California state ballot has been focused on the Billionaire Tax, Prop 40, thanks to heavy-handed spending by a dozen superrich reactionaries who are horrified at the idea that any part of their beyond-Gilded Age-level wealth might get redirected to health care for people who desperately need it. But there are four related measures that require the attention of voters who care about economic inequality and want to address it fairly, since these measures also relate to appropriate taxes for rich people in the Golden State. One, the Education and Health Care Act of 2026 (Prop 3) is a currently existing but temporary income tax on the top two percent of income earners—individuals who make at least $370 thousand, or joint filers who make $740 thousand a year. This top-brackets income tax brought a tidy $14 billion to the state treasury last year. The bulk of its revenue goes to K-12 schools and community colleges. I’ve written previous articles dealing with Prop 3 and so will concentrate on the other three here. 41 and 42: Poison pills for the Billionaire Tax Props 41 and 42 are designed to thwart the Billionaire Tax, and Prop 43, if it passes, will make it very difficult to raise revenue at the local level. Props 41 and 42 were put on the ballot by billionaires hiding behind the anodyne title “Building a Better California” to trick voters into nullifying the billionaire tax. This positive-sounding organization is a PAC funded by right wing ultrarich like Sergey Brin. Prop 41 would supposedly create audits of new state tax revenues and makes them subject to a state cap. The Billionaire Tax will easily earn more than the cap, over which any money is either returned to voters or goes to education. Prop 41 doesn’t mention the Billionaire Tax directly, but it contains a standard California ballot measure poison pill: if it receives more votes than other measures with an overlapping topic (i.e., the Billionaire Tax) it nullifies it. Prop 42 would prohibit new taxes on personal property including retirement accounts, financial assets or business interests. It deceptively proposes that unnamed “Sacramento politicians” are planning to do this to everyone. The only tax it would apply to—again without naming it—is the Billionaire Tax. As with Prop 41, more votes for Prop 42 than 40 nullifies the latter. Let us be very clear. These initiatives aren’t about helping California taxpayers, and they’re not about audits or retirement savings. They are about defeating Prop 40. Knowing who supports a ballot measure as well as who opposes it provides excellent context for understanding its purposes. One of Prop 41 and 42’s main funders is Google founder Sergey Brin, who has recently become the third richest person in the world . Brin has already spent a psychotic $100 million against a tax that would preserve healthcare access for millions of Californians. Other sociopathic billionaires have chipped in $50 million more. Prop 43: a higher barrier for funding local services Proposition 43, also backed by billionaires and corporate entities like the Chamber of Commerce through their shill, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, would impose a supermajority requirement for all local special tax initiatives. It would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. It applies to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027. This new supermajority vote requirement, replacing simple majority for local citizen-initiated measures, would apply to measures raising revenue for all forms of local government—cities, counties, school and community college districts, and any other local or regional government entity. Majority rule is the basis of local democracy. Prop 43, if it passes, would represent a giant step backward, and make it easier for giant corporate interests like the Realtors’ Association, the Chamber of Commerce, fossil fuel companies and other similar entities to wreck funding for the things we all need. Propositions 41, 42, and 43 represent profound threats to California’s future. Putting a lockbox around our cities’ and state’s ability to raise revenue will result in devastating cuts to education, healthcare, public safety and transit and our ability to safely breathe air and drink water. VOTE NO on Propositions 41, 42 and 43.

articles.title: After the Party: Dorothy Healey, Radio Days, and the Reinvention of the Los Angeles Left
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Dorothy Healey (third from right) and other Communists arrested by U.S. Marshals for violating the Smith Act, 1951 (L-R): Unknown, Henry Steinberg, Philip Connelly, Healey, Unknown, Rose Chernin . PART ONE OF TWO On July 9, 1973, Dorothy Healey sat behind a microphone at KPFK in Los Angeles and ended a political commitment that had consumed nearly her entire adult life. She had joined the Young Communist League at 14, organized farmworkers and cannery workers, gone to jail, rose through the ranks of Communist Party leadership, and for two decades led its Southern California district. Now, at 58, she told her radio audience that she was resigning from the party. The immediate cause was almost painfully characteristic of the organization she was leaving. The national party had denounced Al Richmond, the former editor of its West Coast newspaper, the People's World , for his memoir A Long View from the Left . Southern California Communists were instructed to uphold national leaders’ judgment whenever they discussed the book publicly. Healey refused. Her resignation was anything but a renunciation of radical politics. "My hatred of capitalism," she told her listeners, remained as intense as when she had joined the YCL in 1928. She described herself instead as "a communist ... without a party." That distinction would define the rest of her life. Dorothy Healey's political history is often told as a journey from Communism to democratic socialism. The description is accurate but flattens a much, much more interesting story. Beginning with the crisis of world Communism in 1956, Healey spent decades trying to salvage the radicalism, working-class politics, and organizational seriousness of the Communist tradition while discarding authoritarianism, sectarianism, and toeing the party’s foreign policy line. Much of that reinvention happened right here in Los Angeles. From the late 1950s through the early 1980s, Healey occupied an unusual position amongst successive generations of the city's left: the Communist Old Left, the civil rights and antiwar movements, Black and Chicano radicalism, socialist feminism, the New American Movement and finally Democratic Socialists of America. Her story is therefore less about leaving the Communist Party than about the harder question that flowed from it: What do you build after it? The Earthquake of 1956 For American Communists, 1956 was an earthquake. At the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, Nikita Khrushchev exposed a portion of the crimes committed under Joseph Stalin. Healey later remembered hearing the secret speech in New York and being devastated by its revelations. That autumn Soviet tanks crushed the Hungarian uprising, generating debate through out Communist parties around the world. Thousands of Communists in the US responded by voting with their feet and leaving the party. Healey did not. Instead, she became an advocate for democratizing the Communist Party USA from within. That decision made Los Angeles unusually important. Under Healey and her longtime comrade Ben Dobbs, Southern California became a center of dissent, sufficiently independent that the national leadership repeatedly tried and failed to dislodge them. This was not an insignificant backwater club. Healey had been brought into LA’s leadership after World War II and eventually headed what the Los Angeles Times described as the party's second-largest district after New York. The old Popular Front had been broken by the Cold War. Communists had been driven from unions, prosecuted under the Smith Act, blacklisted, surveilled and pushed toward the margins of public life. Healey herself had been convicted under the Smith Act in 1952 before the Supreme Court reversed the California convictions in 1957. Yet Southern California radicalism was already beginning to regenerate outside the party. Civil rights organizers, peace activists, students and young radicals were creating their own political networks. Healey's great post-1956 wager was that the surviving Old Left could enter into conversation with this new one. LA became one of the laboratories. Cover photo from Dorothy Healey’s memoir, California Red, 1990 A Communist on the FM dial In 1959, the same year KPFK began broadcasting in Los Angeles, Dorothy Healey went on the air. The new Pacifica station was itself an experiment. Commercial-free and listener-supported, KPFK gave airtime to an extraordinary range of political opinion, from conservatives such as William F. Buckley and Howard Jarvis to the Communist leader of Southern California. Healey's program, Communist Commentary , gave an avowed Communist a regular voice on the Los Angeles airwaves at the height of the Cold War. Radio suited her. Healey could be ferociously political without sounding mechanical, and she possessed little patience for the wooden language that often passed for Communist public communication. Even critics of her politics encountered something difficult to fit into the stereotype of the obedient party hack: a funny, combative, recognizably local political personality. The program also gave Healey something increasingly important: a political identity larger than the institution she led. As her disagreements with the national Communist Party widened, Angelenos could encounter Dorothy Healey directly, not merely as a representative of the CPUSA. By 1963 her presence at KPFK was prominent enough to become an issue in congressional attacks on Pacifica's broadcasting license. More importantly, KPFK placed Healey inside a rapidly changing Los Angeles political culture. The station became one of the spaces where the Old Left, pacifism, the New Left, feminism, Black radicalism, antiwar activism and the counterculture could collide with one another. Healey no longer had to wait for those movements to enter the Communist Party; she was already talking to them over the radio. That convergence was happening elsewhere in the city as well. Despite the party's losses after 1956, Healey worked to restore relationships with liberals and peace activists and to open the Southern California organization toward younger radicals. Communist youth participated in southern Freedom Rides, and the party's Black membership later developed the Che-Lumumba Club, which became an important political base for Angela Davis. Mike Davis and Jon Wiener have argued that this continuing interaction between Los Angeles's Old and New Lefts distinguishes the city's 1960s history from the familiar national story in which the Communist movement simply disappears before the New Left arrives. Healey became one of the human bridges between those worlds. 1966 Healey campaign button when she ran for Los Angeles County Assessor. Eighty-three thousand votes for a Communist Her peculiar place in Los Angeles politics became visible in 1966, when Healey ran for Los Angeles County Assessor. She made no attempt to disguise her politics. This was a Communist running openly for countywide office less than 15 years after the height of McCarthyism. She received 83,891 votes, 5.4 percent of the total. The result was politically meaningless if measured by winning (and by current DSA LA standards). But it was remarkable as a measure of survival. After blacklists, prosecutions, loyalty investigations and years of official anticommunism, more than 80,000 LA County voters deliberately marked their ballots for Dorothy Healey. The campaign also tells us something about the politics Healey was trying to construct. She was not retreating into a purified revolutionary subculture. She was attempting to make socialism visible within the ordinary political life of Southern California. That strategy put her increasingly at odds with a national party whose instincts remained tied to Moscow and to an increasingly insular organizational culture. Los Angeles Communism had survived the catastrophe of 1956, but the contradiction at its center was becoming harder to contain. Healey wanted the party to open itself toward the new movements; the party leadership continued to demand political reliability. In 1968, the contradiction broke open. Socialism with a Human Face In August 1968, Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia and crushed Prague Spring and Socialismus s Lidskou Tváří (Socialism with a Human Face). Healey had visited the country the previous year and had close connections with Czech communists like Edward and Marta Goldstucker. She condemned the invasion, while Communist Party general secretary Gus Hall and the national leadership defended it. Healey resigned as head of the Southern California district. For Healey, Prague brought the argument that had begun in 1956 to its conclusion. Could socialism exist without democracy? Could a communist movement possess an independent political judgment, or was its loyalty to the foreign policy interests of the Soviet Union ultimately stronger than its commitment to democratic change initiated by other communists? But she still didn’t quit. Healey had spent 40 years in the Communist movement, and a political organization built over a lifetime is not simply a bundle of positions from which one unsubscribes. It was comrades, marriages, campaigns, jail cells, organizing drives, friendships and a way of understanding one's own place in history. So Healey remained inside for another five years, stripped of her old leadership role and increasingly alienated from the national organization. KPFK gave her somewhere else to stand. The microphone allowed Healey to remain a public Marxist while becoming steadily less identifiable with the party hierarchy. A 1972 KPFK recording preserved by the Pacifica archive, for instance, has Healey giving an extended discussion of Rosa Luxemburg, the revolutionary Marxist who had famously battled the bureaucratic and authoritarian tendencies of her own movement and criticized the Bolsheviks even while joining the Spartacists in Germany. Then came July 1973. When the Southern California party instructed its members to repeat the national leadership's attack on Al Richmond, Healey refused one final demand for obedience. She announced her resignation not in a private letter or internal meeting but over KPFK, before the Los Angeles audience she had cultivated for 14 years. The symbolism is almost too neat. Dorothy Healey left the Communist Party through the microphone. [Stay tuned for Part Two in the October California Red .]

articles.title: What is MAC? (A: “A Vehicle for Socialist Change”)
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: OCDSA’s Mutual Aid Committee, affectionately abbreviated to “MAC”, has been one of the chapter’s longest operating undertakings. Following the Marxist ideal of a society sharing goods and services according to ability and need, MAC’s work, directly within the chapter and with members of the community at large, has long been the focus of the group, even before our formal establishment as a committee in 2026. MAC works with community partners to provide meals and groceries to the county’s at-risk and unhoused populations. What does MAC do? In the pandemic years, MAC provided taillight services for free to the community in the wake of George Floyd’s murder, and helped provide groceries to low-income community members directly at their doors during lockdown. Following the easing of social distancing restrictions, MAC worked with community partners to provide meals and groceries to the county’s at-risk and unhoused populations, helped get medical supplies to besieged countries through our partners at Not Just Tourists, established close ties with other mutual aid organizations such as Costa Mesa Mutual Aid, Lucha, and 714 Mutual Aid, and responded to individual requests from members and non-members alike for support with material, emotional, and social needs. What does it take to join MAC? MAC takes a friendly “as you are” approach to service, accepting members regardless of their experience with mutual aid endeavors, and works within their abilities to help empower them through direct work with the community. MAC meets twice a month virtually, provides onsite training at events to help members and volunteers find their footing, and co-hosts events regularly with our community partners. MAC works within the comfortability of our members, taking into consideration people’s interests, capacities, abilities and disabilities, diversity considerations, and opinions to operate horizontally, reciprocally, and in a participatory manner. Grocery packing nights serve as equal parts socials, networking events, and direct actions. How has MAC been a vehicle for socialist change in OC? Because it is the nature of MAC events to involve direct action and accessibility, they are often some of the first events new members attend. Lower-key MAC events like our “cookovers” or grocery packing nights serve as equal parts socials, networking events, and direct actions, while more involved events allow members to interact with orgs outside of DSA to cross-pollinate. MAC has been a powerful tool for OCDSA and its members to demonstrate that we actively stand by our ideals, are friendly with and supportive of the community at large, and that the nurturing, prosocial world that Marx envisioned is possible, even within the belly of the beast What do our members have to say? NH: “Our goal is creating a community where a core value is lifting each other up. We want to build this into the fabric of our community, with systems that provide necessary aid to those in need, with the understanding that at some point, we will also need aid. During my time with OCDSA's Mutual Aid committee, I have had the opportunity to collaborate with other mutual aid groups in OC to foster community and help build and strengthen these systems. The organizing skills I have learned have been invaluable, but even more so, the connections we have made with these incredible people have made a major impact on me. It's been said before that without hope, no one would have the drive to do this work, and I wholeheartedly agree. My cup overflows with hope when I see the overwhelming number of kind-hearted, dedicated people who are activated. If everyone engaged in mutual aid, the world would be a better place, but I also think that every person would be happier, less lonely, and more fulfilled.” PB: “Being a member of MAC is a personal reminder for myself that there’s a need out there, there are like-minded people who want to help fill it, and that though the world can seem discouraging and that I alone can feel powerless to change it, I can at least shape a better place in my corner.” SB: “DSA-MAC is a true demonstration of community and people’s ability to rely on each other when capitalism tries to make everything so scarce and isolated.” ZR: “To me, mutual aid means helping people with what they need without expectations or administrative barriers and being able to be helped when I need it. Being a member of MAC makes me feel like I have a community of people who will support me, and also it gives me space to help others when I am able to and that what I have to give means something.” AL: "As a disabled person I often feel invisible and erased from society. Our needs are often forgotten about by the government and even our fellow man. For me that stopped when I joined the DSA and MAC. As both a member of MAC and someone who benefits from the help it provides, I felt a sense of community that I wasn’t sure was even possible. I felt seen and supported. My comrades put hard work and dedication into our services every week to provide mutual aid to our communities, where like me, people are seen, not discarded."

articles.title: The Revolutionary Cocktail: Why DSA Needs Electoralism, Direct Action, and Mutual Aid to Win
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: PART ONE OF TWO [Reprinted from Geese ] Too often, mutual aid, direct action, and electoralism are treated as exclusive contrasts. Reflecting on his work in the San Diego chapter of DSA, Aldo B. argues that each tactic is part of a necessary whole and that any of them, taken individually, are ineffective as a revolutionary strategy. Abolish ICE May Day 2026. Edgar Ramirez photo A colleague of mine once said that his revolutionary cocktail for the systemic change we needed as a movement entailed three key elements; direct action, mutual aid, and electoralism. This concoction has stuck with me and rolled around in my head since he said it over a year ago in his millennial-style car vlog that he posted on Instagram. I've since expanded these three components into conceptualized processes: Direct Action is the means by which existing conditions are confronted head on to the point of rupture in the mode of production. Mutual-Aid is the logistical metric for satisfying the consumption of a community by an organized grassroots network of distribution and production. Electoralism is the competition between politically organized factions over the attention economy of the electorate, aka, the 30-60% of the population that is allowed to vote. With the recent primaries across the country, my own personal hajj to NYC, and of course the lovely DSA discourse on X the Everything App, this revolutionary cocktail has only come to sit evermore in the front and center of my thinking about how to organize internally around a variety of issues my comrades feel passionately about—especially in light of those issues seemingly being at odds with one another. I’ll state explicitly now that I fundamentally disagree with the framing of these three tactics as being antagonistic towards each other. In fact I would go as far to state that the distilled critiques which a proponent of direct action or mutual aid might level against electoralism and a staunch electoralist against the proponents of mutual aid or direct action, are all the same. None of these tactics are an end in and of themselves. Standing alone, Mutual-Aid is mere charity at best, or bandaids for bullet holes at its worst; Direct Action is frankly adventurism at best, or in the worst case acts as a revolutionary release valve; and Electoralism may demonstrate a shift in the Overton Window, but at the expense of cooptation and complacency with a tepid reformism. It is only together, united by a coherent and democratically decided strategy, that its potency for revolutionary change can be actualized. That's enough theory for now, but I want this conceptual engine to be humming in the background as you read this piece. DSA contingent at Progressive Labor Summit 2026. Random attendee photo Personally, since I was a young man, I have always strived to be a well-rounded organizer, a Jack of All Trades if you will. My mother would call me a metiche (nosey?), but that's neither here nor there. The way that manifests in my organizing today is that I have a tendency to stick my fingers in every pie within arm’s reach. I run the political education committee as an elected leader in my chapter, founded and am an active participant of our migrant rights subcommittee, am the former mentor for the electoral working group and current campaign manager of a chapter cadre campaign, a proud member of the Springs of Revolution network championing our national priority Labor for an Arms Embargo locally in conjunction with our Palestine Solidarity and Labor working groups; and last, but certainly not least, my day job is as an organizer for a statewide non-profit that leans towards tenant organizing. All that to say is, six years into my organizing journey, I have yet to pigeonhole myself into just one avenue of organizing. I may not have done it consciously initially, but I try to embody the concoction of this revolutionary formula in my day-to-day organizing projects. Through my experience, I believe there is something to be abstracted from the overlaps in these tactically diverse projects and campaigns.Allow me to explain. I will start with direct action as it is probably the most contentious and certainly the most volatile element of the cocktail. I want to clarify now that I am not necessarily talking about the high-risk civil disobedience operations of a Palestine Action or of a civil uprising nature; though assuredly those too have their place in the cocktail. The primary methods of direct action organized by DSA San Diego are pro-Palestine banner drops, anti-ICE community defense, and strike line support. In my opinion, banner drops are a sort of guerrilla political education and agitation. Of the near dozen banner drops we have organized or supported in the last year, they have proven to be opportunities for some of the most frank organizing conversations amongst the membership and with the general public. I recall one instance during a banner drop in the South Bay, a predominantly Latine working class community, where a woman began to lightly criticize us; not for being pro-Palestine, but genuinely interrogating us as to how hanging a piece of painted cloth over a bridge helps the Palestinian people. The working group cochair and I explained to her that our intentions were to keep Palestine in the public’s mind. Nearly three years into the genocide and almost a year into Trump’s regime, it almost feels as though, with the onslaught of tragedy after tragedy domestically, people might forget or deprioritize Palestinian liberation in order to deal with the struggles we have to overcome at home. What we were really trying to do was emphasize that the struggle in Palestine was the same struggle we faced here. ICE Rapid Response First Aid Training. Antonio Raass photo In the same vein, our anti-ICE community patrols are another form of direct action. Just as in Palestine the genocide was result of a century of development by the Zionist entity, experimenting with different methods of occupation and disenfranchisement, Trump and the Department of Homeland Security are fomenting the early stages of an ethnic cleansing of working class black and brown people from our communities. When I motivated to prioritize community self-defense in the chapter, I was met with some well-intentioned pushback. The main worry was the high-risk nature of the work and associating with organizations like Union del Barrio (which had just been the target of a congressional investigation for their role in the LA resistance to ICE occupation). Ultimately, enough members of the working group reasoned that, if DSA defending migrant communities was unlawful, then that long arm would eventually come for us anyway. We spent the first three months investigating how radical projects like this had been executed in the past. We examined the Black Panthers and engaged with the plethora of resources that organizations like CrimeThinc, SiempraNC, and Front Line Defenders had compiled on ICE tactics and strategy. We read historical and contemporary pieces of theory on how a ragtag group of socialists could even stand a chance at hampering in any way an imperial terror machine like the US government. As we grew and developed, we realized that patrolling the community was beginning to inspire discourse on the notion and structures of public safety. This consciousness was spreading not just among patrollers, but within the communities themselves. The patrols became prefigurative for how a community protects itself from an entity that wishes to do it harm, and our chapter was a driving force in that. Direct action also takes the form of labor work. We are lucky enough locally to have a talented and knowledgeable labor working group chair that keeps tabs on every union in contract negotiations, prepping for a strike, or already on the strike line. By the time they have begun, we are already actively organizing in support of it. We are turning out members to the strike line, donating to strike funds, and even anchoring strike kitchens. My experience walking strike lines has displayed (and tested) the vast spectrum of revolutionary optimism that can emerge out of solidarity with militant workers fighting against unfair labor practices. It is almost a form of political education similar to what occurs during a banner drop, except no one is wondering what exactly the picketers are trying to accomplish—it’s right there on the signs! Most recently, on a 24-hour Teamsters picket line, I got to talk to workers about everything from the world cup to the Iran war. But the most consistent topic the workers brought up was that, in spite of the risk they were taking, they felt deeply convinced that they could win this fight. It was deeply inspirational and to my mind demonstrated the potency of direct action as not just a tactic for fighting the good fight, but as a method for motivating workers that a better world was in fact possible. All they needed was to take the risk to fight for it. [Stay tuned for Part Two in the October California Red ]
