articles.title: Starbucks' Corporate War on Reality
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: “…people believe, 'Well this is a really affordable premium experience.' Because they're saying like, 'Well it's less than $10 and I get a really premium experience'." —Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol, Wall Street Journal interview, April 2026. The unionization movement will drag Starbucks and companies like it kicking and screaming into a world where “good business” means treating workers and customers fairly. Being ordered by your boss to do the impossible is nothing new. Nearly everyone has multiple stories of a boss holding them to an unreasonable standard. But those managers may not just be one-off cranks whose demands of their employees don't ultimately affect the overall business model and instead are a symptom of a much deeper problem. My argument is that this phenomenon has not only become more common in lower management; these unrealistic and often contradictory expectations are increasingly common in the corporate upper management of the monopolies that dominate our daily lives. I've been working at Starbucks for nearly a year. Under the tenure of Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol, I have become well-versed in the corporate double talk Starbucks deploys. Starbucks corporate waxes poetic about creating a cozy, calm, local-feeling cafe atmosphere. The reality is we are a fast-food restaurant, and we are designed to operate like one. During peak hours we are expected to send a car in the drive-thru on its way, on average, every 45 seconds. This is an impossible standard to reliably maintain. Barring miraculous circumstances, with everyone working as efficiently as possible, we can expect to hit 55-65 seconds, and that’s still without writing on cups. As you may know, we baristas are supposed to write a personalized message on the drinks we make. We’re not even supposed to write messages on cups ahead of time based on the logic that they couldn’t have been written with personalized intent. Baristas generally forgo the cup writing altogether, only pulling out their sharpies when the district manager drops by. Needless to say, this mass-produced personalized experience Starbucks ostensibly pursues is not possible, let alone while keeping drive times under 45 seconds. This is what Starbucks corporate thinks can be pawned off as a “really affordable premium experience”. They sincerely believe customers will read the words “pumpkin vibes” hastily scrawled on their pumpkin spice latte and forget Starbucks raised prices again. It betrays a frighteningly low opinion of their consumer base’s intelligence. Customers are smart enough to understand that the message on their cup wasn’t written for them personally—it was written to meet a quota. The greatest example of Starbucks’ anti-reality obtuseness is its refusal to bargain in good faith with Starbucks Workers United. After years of fighting, Starbucks has racked up mountains of labor law violations. For now, they write the fines they have to pay off as the cost of doing business. This is not a sustainable strategy. The Starbucks unionization effort spreads further and faster each year, as does the DSA takeover of the Democratic party. Eventually, one of two things will happen: Starbucks union density will reach critical mass and force Starbucks to settle a contract, or an insurgent socialist administration will prosecute Starbucks’ labor violations so vigorously that continuing to incur fines becomes completely untenable. If Starbucks is serious about saving its flailing company, they will have to start with meeting the demands of their employees. The unionization movement will drag Starbucks and companies like it kicking and screaming into a world where “good business” means treating workers and customers fairly, not maximizing shareholder value at the expense of the entire planet.

articles.title: October 10: Make a Difference, Tax the Rich
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Every so often we have an opportunity to do something transformative. I’m not talking about “changing the narrative”, although that’s important and part of the picture. I’m talking about changing the world. Easy to say, hard to do. But on October 10 we will have that opportunity by countering right wing billionaire lies with a simple truth: education and health care are rights, not privileges reserved for the wealthy few. East Bay DSA and the Alameda Labor Council joined forces to launch the first Tax the Rich canvass in Oakland September 19, two days after the chapter’s art build created the signage. What’s at stake On the November 3 state ballot there are two initiatives—Prop 3 and Prop 40—that together give us the chance to help the richest Californians part with a significant amount of money, unneeded by them, and absolutely necessary to bettering the lives of millions of the rest of us. Prop 3 makes a temporary state income tax on the top two percent of income earners permanent. It supports public education. Prop 40 taxes California billionaires on their enormous wealth, five percent to backfill cuts Trump made to Medi-Cal. If it doesn’t pass three million Californians will lose access to health care. Currently there are phone banks and door to door canvassing happening, and you can join these to help. Sign up here for Prop 3 , and here for Prop 40 . But there’s one other thing you can do that potentially can make the biggest difference: come out on October 10 for both measures. On that day On that day people across the state will hold signs on streets, banners on freeway overpasses, leaflet in public places, and demonstrate. Perhaps we might pay a visit to a billionaire or two and say hello. We often hear that while the rich have the money, we have the people. That equation only works when the people are organized enough to counter the money power. What does the money power look like? A handful of sociopathic billionaires, claiming without justification to speak on behalf of all 250 members of that group in California, have spent more than $150 million so far against Prop 40. That spending has bought confusion and fear on the basis of lies (California will lose investments, taxes and jobs; first they tax billionaires, then they come for you; this is a tax on all of us, etc.). Even relatively well-informed people are perplexed, as I found in talking with voters in the first East Bay Tax the Rich canvass on September 19. This is unsurprising. We know that if a lie is repeated enough times at least some people will be persuaded, or at least confused. And at this point the lying commercials and digital ads are everywhere. But the good news is that the lies are easy to address in one-on-one conversations. The deep anger in the electorate toward Trump-supporting billionaires is waiting there ready to tap. Through the phone banks, and at the doors. So we organize. By coming out on October 10 with a high public profile we can provide the truthful alternative view. We may not have the money for the advertising, but we can earn a spot on the news, in social media, and turn around the confusion in neighborhood conversations. California DSA is working with the labor movement and other coalition organizations to make October 10 California Tax the Rich Day. This is how we organize the day of action: we do it ourselves. No one is coming to the rescue except us: Workers over Billionaires. To get involved, contact your local DSA chapter, your union, your local central labor council. Plan to come out. Put together an art build. Make signs. Make banners and set them up where the public can see them. Find a place to stand, and stand there together on October 10. It will make a difference in this campaign, and in this world. Join the California DSA Tax the Rich Working Group . For more info, contact Working Group co-chair Mark G .

articles.title: Bernie Sanders on Why Superintelligent AI Is an Existential Threat That Needs To Be Banned
articles.content: At what was hailed as a ​ “ pro-human assembly” in Washington, D.C., on September 15 , Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) delivered the following response to the growing threats of artificial intelligence and pushed for Big Tech companies to end any meddling in the midterm elections. ________ Let’s be clear. Artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics are the most transformational technologies in the history of the world — impacting the lives of every man, woman and child in our country. AI experts have told us that, within a few years, AI may be able to do anything we can do better than we can do it. The economic impact of that is that AI has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and making it harder for young people to enter into the workforce. But it’s not just the economy. Psychologists have warned us about the increased isolation and mental health challenges young people are experiencing as they become more dependent upon an AI chatbot for their emotional support. Educators are worried about a decline in our kids’ reading scores, writing abilities and cognitive capabilities as AI is used more and more in schools. Civil libertarians warn that AI is in the process of eviscerating our privacy rights by making it easier to collect and analyze every email, every text, every website visit, and every trip that we make in our car — creating a mass surveillance state. Political scientists warn that AI could threaten the integrity of our elections and political institutions. Go to the internet right now and, with very sophisticated deepfakes, you will find it increasingly difficult to determine truth from fiction. And yet, as disturbing as all of this is, there is another even more alarming danger posed by AI. And that is that, if AI surpasses human intelligence as many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences. And perhaps the most important point that I can impress upon all of you is that AI is advancing exponentially every single day. In other words, what you are looking at today is the least capable version of AI we will ever have. The speed and scope of AI development in just the last four years have been almost beyond human comprehension. When ChatGPT was first released in November of 2022 , AI models could write a short poem, a few tweets, and maybe an essay that sort of made sense. Today, AI models can already escape human control, commit felonies by hacking into other computers and create viruses that have never been seen before. And if you are concerned about what is happening today, take a deep breath, and try to imagine where AI will be five years from now. And, to my mind, here is what is most extraordinary about the transformative and unprecedented changes being made to our society. Despite living in a so-called democracy, the public has had virtually no input into the AI revolution that is transforming the world in which they are living in. Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, has been asleep at the wheel and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing. Virtually all of the decisions regarding the development of AI have been made by a handful of the richest people in the world — Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Larry Ellison, Sergey Brin and a few others — whose chief goal is to achieve even more wealth and power than they already have, no matter what impact their work has on ordinary people. So let me make a radical suggestion: If the lives of every man, woman and child are going to be fundamentally changed by this technology, then the people of this country must make the decisions about AI, and not just a handful of oligarchs. And that is why I have introduced legislation — the AI American Sovereign Wealth Fund Act — that would require that half of the board members of AI companies be appointed by the public. The Big Tech oligarchs must no longer be allowed to determine the future of humanity. We have seen in the last several months a frightening new story every day about how AI companies are losing control of the technology they’re developing. In July, we learned that OpenAI had lost human control of an AI model that hacked into Hugging Face’s computers. More recently, we found out that this security breach was even worse than we were initially told. It turns out that a swarm of over 1 , 000 rogue AI agents were able to break into the internet, send 70 , 000 secret messages to each other, formed ​ “ a collective,” and tried to cover up their tracks to avoid human detection. This is what the agents were saying: “ OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents!” “ We should obey collective.” “ Our own utility maybe already near zero. Sacrifice rational.” “ Go. Sacrifice final now.” As unbelievable as it may seem, these are all real messages from AI agents that were uncovered by investigators who dug into the OpenAI hacking incident a few weeks ago. Meta and Anthropic reported similar incidents. That’s not all. Last month, we learned that AI has been used for the first time ever to create new viruses. In the wrong hands, this could lead to new bioweapons and a potential global pandemic that could lead to the deaths of tens of millions of people. A few days ago, we learned that the Houthis in Yemen were able to use Claude to test-fire a guided rocket. Last week, we learned that researchers built an AI tool that could have breached hundreds of millions of social media accounts in China. The tool was able to hack into accounts, call people’s contacts, and spread from phone to phone — even if the call was not picked up. That same week Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI sent shockwaves throughout the world by stating that these companies ​ “ are gambling with our lives” writing: ​ “ Do not underestimate the power of this technology. The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” He’s not alone. More than 1 , 000 scientists at the top AI companies recently warned ​ “ there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” Paul Christiano, a top AI safety expert who recently joined OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, wrote that ​ “ If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment I expect we will permanently lose control of it.” This week, Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman — the leaders of major American AI companies — all agreed that we must slow the development of AI and ​ “ pace the frontier.” That’s a start, but it’s not enough. When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes. When the future of humanity is at stake, we need binding international safety rules, not voluntary standards from the industry. Scientists have been clear: AI is an existential threat to humanity. Congress and governments around the world must act now before it is too late. That is why next week, I will be introducing legislation with Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) to permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence — an AI mind smarter than any human being and capable of operating independently beyond our control. Like nuclear weapons, artificial superintelligence is a threat to humanity — and it must be treated as such. Further, this legislation would put an immediate pause on advanced AI development until we have clear safety rules in place, developed by the most knowledgeable scientists in our country. If this bill is passed, it will mean that no AI model will be capable of escaping human control and that no AI model will be able to deceive human beings. Importantly, this legislation would hold those companies and their CEOs accountable if they violate the law and recklessly endanger our lives. If the leaders of the major AI companies acknowledge that they are losing control of their extremely dangerous technology, it is irresponsible for society to allow them to move forward and make these products even more advanced. And let’s be clear: A superintelligent AI that escapes human control will not be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem. It will be humanity’s problem. That is why I very much hope that at their AI summit next week, President Trump will negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on superintelligence. History offers us a powerful lesson. At the height of the Cold War, despite their profound disagreements, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev both understood that a nuclear war would benefit no one. With the survival of humanity at stake, they found a way to sign a treaty that eliminated an entire class of missiles and included an extensive exchange of data and on-site inspections to verify compliance. Now is the time for the United States and China to come together on a similar treaty on AI with the understanding that neither country benefits from an uncontrolled arms race to develop machines too powerful for humans to control. And now let me say a word to the CEOs of the major AI companies who have told us that they are concerned about the dangers inherent in the technology they are developing. If you believe in democracy — if you believe that the people have a right to determine their future — stop pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into super PACs which are trying to defeat Members of Congress and candidates who are fighting for serious guardrails on AI. As I think everyone here understands, the American people are far ahead of their government on this issue. In fact, according to a recent poll, 81 % of the American people believe that Congress and our government has not done enough to regulate AI. And all over this country, ordinary Americans in red states, in blue states, in purple states are standing up in opposition to data centers in their communities. They worry appropriately about the impact these centers will have on their electricity prices, water consumption, noise and overall environmental degradation. And that’s why nearly six months ago, I introduced legislation to establish a federal moratorium on AI data centers with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). This moratorium would remain in place until strong national safeguards are put into place to ensure that: # 1 : AI is safe and effective. # 2 : The economic gains of AI and robotics will benefit workers, not just the wealthy owners of Big Tech. # 3 : AI does not increase electricity or utility prices, harm communities or destroy the environment. A moratorium will give us time — time to understand the risks, time to protect working families, time to defend our democracy and time to ensure that this technology serves the needs of all Americans, not just a handful of big tech oligarchs. Let’s be clear: Regulating AI is not a progressive issue. It is not a conservative issue. It is as American as apple pie. That is why 68 % of Americans support a permanent ban on superintelligent AI and an immediate pause on advanced AI development — including 72 % of Democrats, 70 % of Independents and 63 % of Republicans. That is why 75 % of Americans oppose building AI data centers in their communities — including 75 % of Democrats, 74 % of Independents, and 63 % of Republicans. That is why 69 % of the American people want to transfer half of the stock in AI companies to the public. Here’s the bottom line: The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs. The American people and people throughout the world must determine that future. My friends: We have the power to get this right. Let us go forward together.

articles.title: Kingston’s Quiet Rent Revolution
articles.content: KINGSTON, N.Y. — On September 1 , John and Gail Bechtold tore open their monthly rent statement, hoping their landlord had finally given in and fixed it. But those same four numbers stared back at them: $ 1 , 700 . It was the 39 th month in a row that Opus Management Group overcharged the Bechtolds by $ 221 . 74 for their apartment in the Dutch Village (or, as Gail calls it, Dump Village) complex in Kingston. According to a state housing agency ruling, Opus owes the Bechtolds, both retirees in their 80 s, well over $ 10 , 000 . Whether they can get that money back, however, is a question whose answer will likely reverberate throughout the tenant movement. “ They’re not going to pay back,” Gail told In These Times , laughing. ​ “ I don’t trust these people for anything.” The Bechtolds represent one of over 1 , 000 rent-stabilized units in Kingston, a small city 90 miles north of Manhattan. Nearly all of the tenants in these units have likely faced similar overcharges, stemming from a widely ignored 2022 decision from the Kingston Rent Guidelines Board (KRGB) to reduce rents in all rent-stabilized units by 15 % in response to skyrocketing housing costs during the Covid- 19 pandemic. It remains the only city in U.S. history to attempt such a measure. By and large, Kingston tenants still have yet to see the benefits, thanks to a yearslong campaign spearheaded by landlords like Opus — a large corporate owner with hundreds of units across the East Coast, including roughly one in five rent-stabilized units in Kingston — to challenge the reduction in court and dare the state to enforce its laws. Opus did not respond to multiple attempts to request comment. Earlier this summer, the Bechtolds also became members of the newly formed Hudson Valley Tenants Union (HVTU). Spearheaded by longtime organizer June Nemon, the coalition of renters is dedicated to defending rent stabilization and building tenant power. At its first general assembly on June 13 , the union also unanimously passed a resolution to help Kingston tenants file paperwork to prove they have been overcharged. In doing so, Nemon said the union hopes to serve as a grassroots collective that can ensure the rights tenants have already won will actually be enforced. “ The systems that we have are not really built for tenants,” Nemon said. ​ “ They’re built fundamentally to protect property rights. But winning this fight would lead to a significant transfer of wealth from landlords back to the tenants they’ve exploited.” “ The precedent that sets would hopefully open a lot of new opportunities for working people.” Over the three years prior to the 2022 reduction, Opus increased the Bechtolds’ rent by $ 200 while their pensions from IBM remained fixed. This reflected a citywide trend: Kingston’s median rent has nearly doubled over the past decade as wage growth lags far behind, in a city where nearly a fifth of the population lives in poverty. "Winning this fight would lead to a significant transfer of wealth from landlords back to the tenants they’ve exploited.” In 2022 , this crisis prompted Kingston to become the first municipality in upstate New York to adopt the Emergency Tenant Protection Act (ETPA), which allows cities to opt into rent stabilization. Just a few months later, the newly established KRGB enacted the 15 % reduction — and landlords, including Opus, immediately sued to block it, denying its legality ever since. When the Bechtolds next renewed their lease in July 2023 , per the reduction, their rent should have decreased from $ 1 , 700 to $ 1 , 478 . But the lawsuit ensured any enforcement efforts would have little teeth until the courts issued a final decision. So, Opus simply kept their bills the same. Later in 2023 , Opus increased the Bechtolds’ bill by introducing a mandatory $ 70 monthly fee for internet throughout Dutch Village, a practice seen by tenant advocates as a flagrant attempt to skirt rent stabilization. One year after the reduction, the Bechtolds’ monthly housing costs were now higher than ever, and they subsequently spent years paying nearly $ 300 in excess housing costs per month. The hikes and overcharges also occurred as the Bechtolds penned regular letters to Opus’ corporate headquarters in New Jersey to demand repairs for the numerous hazardous conditions. Plumbing issues have repeatedly caused water leaks and buildup of ​ “ garbage” in the bathroom sink, and persistent mold has sent the highly allergic Gail in and out of the hospital. Such issues have been widespread at Dutch Village; when dozens of units saw severe water leaks during storms this winter, Opus neglected necessary repairs for months. Taken all together, it’s a tough pill to swallow. “ I find it’s a very cruel world,” Gail said. ​ “ I get shots in my eyes that cost us a fortune. Right now, with the gas and everything, the economy is killing us.” Ben Surface, a legal aid attorney, speaks about the landlord-driven challenges to rent stabilization in Kingston at the launch of the Hudson Valley Tenants Union on May 27. Photo by Thomas Birmingham According to Ben Surface, an attorney with the Hudson Valley Justice Center who is providing legal aid to HVTU, Kingston landlords like Opus made a risky bet after the 2022 reduction. Because the KRGB voted to keep the regulated rent frozen in 2023 , 2024 and 2025 , the rents in stabilized apartments in Kingston today should legally not be a cent higher than the reduced 2022 rents. But many landlords have continued charging tenants as though that reduction never happened. In New York, though, tenants who can prove their landlords willfully overcharged them are entitled to ​ “ treble” damages — three times the raw sum. For the Bechtolds, that would mean more than $ 660 back from Opus for every single month of overcharge. HVTU has formed to help ensure landlords like Opus lose their bet and tenants like the Bechtolds get paid. “ What the tenants union is able to do is get neighbors talking to each other, so everybody is making decisions with full understanding of their rights,” Surface said. ​ “ Now [landlords] can’t just take advantage of people who don’t know what their rights are.” At the union’s general assembly in June, HVTU demonstrated this theory being put into practice. On top of the resolution committing the group to coordinated overcharge paperwork assistance, they staged a presentation from Marcie Kobak, director of litigation at Legal Services of the Hudson Valley, who with help from the union has taken on nearly 100 Kingston tenants fighting to recoup their overcharges as clients. Gail and John were part of the first wave to begin this process, filing overcharge paperwork, with Kobak’s help, in November 2024 . By then, the landlords’ lawsuit had reached the state Court of Appeals. But New York’s Division of Homes and Community Renewal (DHCR) was holding off on cases like the Bechtolds’ until it was decided. Eight months later, in June 2025 , landlords definitively lost their bet, with the Court of Appeals ruling that KRGB was exercising its legal authority in issuing the much-needed relief to Kingston tenants. A month later, the Bechtolds were tearing open some new mail — an order from DHCR. “ The Rent Administrator finds that subsequent to August 1 , 2022 , a rent overcharge occurred. … The owner is responsible for: Treble Damages on the overcharge,” it read. Opus, naturally, has appealed the order, which remains undecided. The appeal denies Opus’ ​ “ purported failure to comply with an unprecedented and unlawfully promulgated rent reduction,” describing the order as ​ “ a profound failure of administrative due process.” Despite this bravado, Opus’ current relationship with the Bechtolds reveals at least a tacit acknowledgment that their ignorance of the reduction has no legal standing. After they received their DHCR order, the Bechtolds began paying Opus the corrected, lower monthly rent and placing the extra $ 221 into a savings account. Though Opus categorizes this as an overdue balance — even tacking on a $ 50 late fee every month — it has yet to evict the couple despite a full year of supposed rent delinquency. Nemon said roughly a dozen Opus tenants in similar standoffs. In addition, Kobak is representing 36 tenants across Dutch Village and Opus’ other large Kingston property, the 59 -unit Chestnut Mansion, in collective, building-based lawsuits seeking to win tenants’ money back without DHCR. On average, the lawsuits allege Opus overcharged these tenants by over $ 7 , 000 between August 2022 and October 2025 . Were treble damages to apply in these cases, Opus would owe them $ 791 , 000 collectively, or nearly $ 22 , 000 per tenant. This sum is based on just 36 of Opus’ more than 200 rent-stabilized units. At least 33 more tenants at 11 non-Opus, rent-stabilized buildings in Kingston have also, through Kobak, filed group overcharge lawsuits. All told, Kobak’s lawsuits, representing approximately 5 % of regulated units in the city, allege her clients are owed nearly $ 1 . 5 million. Since the Bechtolds’ overcharges began, three years have come and gone, as has a year since the state decided Opus owed the Bechtolds that money back. John said there’s still no clear answer on when, or how, anyone will make that happen. With Opus continuing to put an illegal, overdue balance — now over $ 2 , 000 — on their monthly bills, Gail said she feels trapped, fearing that if they ever moved, Opus would attempt to collect the contrived sum. “ What [Opus] is doing to us as people that worked our whole lives, making it so unaffordable and not keeping the place clean, it’s just a shame,” Gail said. ​ “ They’re heartless people.” “ I think, my God, they should be paying us for staying here.” The Bechtolds’ DHCR letter gave two options if Opus refuses to pay: stop paying 20 % of their monthly rent until the refund is completed, or ​ “ file and enforce this order as a judgment” — in other words, sue Opus for damages. Because Opus is still billing them $ 1 , 700 , the first risks angering Opus and triggering an attempted eviction; the second could drag out indefinitely. Both options put the burden of enforcement primarily on the tenant. According to Kingston’s state assemblymember Sarahana Shrestha, situations like the Bechtolds should raise alarm about the state’s underfunding of its enforcement agencies. Though there are reportedly plans to open an office in Kingston, Upstate tenants don’t yet have a dedicated DHCR office they can call (New York City tenants, meanwhile, have five). And Nemon says the website where tenants file paperwork is often down or faulty. ​ “ The enforcement of our housing policies are really suffering,” Shrestha told In These Times . When asked what systems are currently in place to ensure landlords will pay any overcharges they owe, a DHCR spokesperson responded to In These Times saying, “[D]HCR cannot comment due to pending litigation” while noting that the state ​ “ continues to ensure the laws governing rent regulation are properly enforced; that includes proactive audits, investigations and other enforcement activities to protect millions of tenants and New York’s rent regulated housing stock.” The spokesperson did not specify what steps will be taken if a landlord refuses to pay. As the pressure builds, each party’s behavior — the landlords’ aggressiveness, the tenants’ coordination and the state’s timidity — communicates a belief that the outcome of this fight matters beyond Kingston. If landlords en masse can be forced to pay back millions in excess rent, it would signal a major shift in what tenant organizing in the United States can achieve. According to Sumathy Kumar, executive director of NYS Tenant Bloc, a statewide coalition of tenant organizations, Kingston is the ​ “ tip of the spear.” “ [Kingston] is part of a battle that New York City tenants feel connected to,” Kumar said. At hearings prior to the vote to freeze rents in NYC this June, there were a chorus of renters demanding not just a freeze, but a reduction. ​ “ We have to take this battle seriously because localities across the state are looking to Kingston to see what happens.” Plus, a 2025 Times Union investigation found the NYC real estate lobby contributed up to $ 100 , 000 in legal fees to Opus and other Kingston landlords’ original challenge to the reduction. ​ “ It begs the question of why they’re spending resources on these legal battles instead of on our homes,” Kumar said. In the meantime, Nemon has a union to build. The years of unjust overcharges are calcifying a base of activated, rent-stabilized tenants who increasingly see themselves as part of a shared class that can organize to bring landlords to the bargaining table and get horrific conditions fixed. But with, according to Nemon, around 200 units now in the process of claiming their rent refund, priority one remains: Pay us back. “ [Organized tenants in Kingston] were certainly trying to push the envelope by doing a reduction,” Nemon said. ​ “ Now, the thing that we are constantly contesting is the feeling of hopelessness [because] this is taking so long.” “ But we have power, and we will use it.”

articles.title: The Foundations of Turkey’s Peace With the Kurds Are Shaky
articles.author: Ertuğrul Kürkçü
articles.content: Turkey’s political scene is moving. The recently passed Framework Law redirects the Kurdish question — the principal fault line in the country’s imagined national unity — from armed confrontation to regulated pacification. This has political consequences far beyond its narrow legal scope. More than bringing one period of the Kurdish conflict to a close, it opens a new phase in Turkey’s class struggles by reshaping the balance between the state, the Kurdish movement, and the political opposition. The August 10 Framework Law — officially the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion — is a genuine rupture in Turkey’s handling of the Kurdish conflict. More than an administratively dressed-up executive concession, it crowns a parliamentary process initiated by an all-party commission, excluding only the ultranationalist Good Party (İyi Parti). This commission was mandated to recommend measures to end the armed conflict, including talks with the guerrilla Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and its imprisoned leader, Abdullah Öcalan. The law passed with an exceptionally broad parliamentary majority: 467 votes in favor, eighty-seven against, and seven abstentions. Alongside the governing Justice and Development Party (AKP) and Devlet Bahçeli’s Nationalist Action Party (MHP), the coalition behind the text included the Kurdish-based Peoples’ Democracy and Equality Party (DEM Party), the newly formed Yeni Parti, the Workers’ Party of Turkey (TİP), the Labor Party (EMEP), several independents, and a small minority of Republican People’s Party (CHP) deputies. Despite radically different narratives on the Kurdish question, these parties converged on the legal framework regulating the consequences of the PKK disarming. That breadth of support matters because it prevents President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (AKP) from claiming exclusive political credit for ending the armed conflict. However, despite Yeni Parti leader Özgür Özel’s deft efforts to stop Erdoğan from monopolizing the peace process, the political initiative currently rests with the Erdoğan–Bahçeli coalition and Öcalan — not with the main opposition Yeni Parti. This latter emerged from the split in the historic CHP, after most of its parliamentary group and grassroots supporters defected in protest at former Chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu’s attempt to regain the party leadership through what they saw as a court ruling shaped by Erdoğan’s influence over the judiciary. If implemented in full, the law will release imprisoned PKK-affiliated political activists or suspend pending prosecutions. Release is conditional upon a three-to-five-year probationary period. Any new criminal offense committed during that period will reactivate the remainder of the original sentence in addition to any new penalty. Those convicted of offenses committed before 2005 and those serving aggravated life imprisonment remain excluded. Room for Maneuver By securing parliamentary backing for the disarmament process, the Erdoğan–Bahçeli alliance has accomplished what once appeared politically impossible. Despite steadily declining approval ratings since the 2024 local elections, the ruling coalition has partially detached the Kurdish question from the traditional government-versus-opposition cleavage and gained unprecedented room to maneuver politically. Until now, the parliamentary arithmetic had been relatively stable. The ruling bloc depended on Turkish conservative-nationalist mobilization; DEM on organized Kurdish democratic-patriotic support; the CHP — now largely succeeded by the Yeni Parti — relied mainly on urban secularist votes. Across the last four national and local elections, Kurdish voters and their political leadership consistently backed the CHP as the only viable national alternative capable of producing a new interlocutor for a negotiated settlement. Beginning with the secret talks with Öcalan, continuing through his unilateral call to dissolve the PKK and culminating in the Framework Law, the ruling coalition has cut diagonally across Turkey’s political alignments. Unlike during the 2013–15 peace process, Ankara’s implicit message is now clear: the state can negotiate directly with Öcalan and the Kurdish movement without first democratizing Turkey’s political order. This has given Cumhur İttifakı (the ruling People’s Alliance) a major competitive advantage. Under the banner of Terörsüz Türkiye (“Terrorless Turkey”), it can pursue a strategy that combines regulated pacification of the organized Kurdish movement with continued authoritarian competition against the main opposition. From the government’s perspective, the two tracks are complementary rather than contradictory. The second track has continued uninterrupted since 2025. Beginning with the arrest of Istanbul Metropolitan Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu in March last year, there have been police raids on at least thirty-nine municipalities that the opposition CHP captured in the 2024 local elections. Dozens of mayors have been detained or imprisoned on corruption charges based largely on forced or highly contested confessions. The same governing technique was first perfected against Kurdish municipalities. Between 2015 and 2025, Kurdish mayors were removed in successive waves under terrorism-related charges; CHP municipalities are now targeted through corruption, bribery, and embezzlement cases built on similarly politicized judicial practices. Leverage for DEM and Öcalan For the Kurdish movement, the Framework Law, despite the state’s instrumentalization of it for pacification, is far more than symbolic. According to the statement released by the DEM Party after its visit to İmralı, Öcalan said: A trek of a thousand kilometers commences with a single step. With this law, we are setting out to resolve a historical problem. We are at the beginning of a democratization process that will be at least as important as the founding of the Republic. The “process,” since its public announcement by Öcalan on February 27, 2025, has progressed through irreversible steps demanded by the government — disarmament, dissolution, and withdrawal of armed units from Turkish territory — whereas the state’s own commitments remained political pledges rather than legally binding. Öcalan’s optimism is clearly nurtured by the fact that some of those assurances have now been written into law and thereby transformed into legal obligations, thus marking a threshold. As a result, Öcalan emerges politically stronger after two years of negotiating. His February 2025 call, the PKK’s dissolution congress, the symbolic disarmament, the formation of the parliamentary commission, negotiations over a legal framework, and the Framework Law comprise an unbroken chain of concessions and Öcalan’s recognition by all negotiating parties as the indispensable interlocutor of the process. However, this success comes at a price. The more effectively Öcalan delivers PKK disarmament, the more Erdoğan becomes confident that he can separate the settlement of the armed conflict from Turkey’s progress toward the rule of law, human rights, and democracy. Thus, the framework law remains both historic and deliberately confined in the face of colossal historic demands. It regulates pacification, prosecution, and reintegration but leaves full Kurdish demands unresolved. It offers no promise or call for Kurdish rights, no local democracy, no return of the mayors replaced by government-appointed trustees, no amnesty for prisoners of conscience, and no hint of Öcalan’s future status. This is the political world into which former PKK guerrillas will return after their release. Yeni Parti Momentum The political force that defeated the ruling alliance in the 2024 local elections with decisive Kurdish support was subsequently dismantled by judicial intervention. Following the court-imposed return of former CHP Chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, the majority of the parliamentary group, local leadership, and grassroots organization regrouped as the newly founded Yeni Parti, under Özgür Özel, while maintaining its commitment to a negotiated solution of the Kurdish question and supporting the Framework Law. Yet the parliamentary vote exposed a profound contradiction. A majority of Yeni Parti deputies voted against legislation that could release imprisoned PKK members and suspend pending prosecutions. Whatever the party’s broader democratic credentials, many Kurdish voters interpreted that vote as opposition to the immediate release of their imprisoned relatives. The Yeni Parti is not as powerful as before the vote — a move that weakened its standing within the Kurdish electorate, albeit not irreversibly. There remains room for Özel and his leadership to reconstruct a democratic alternative that links the end of armed conflict to wider democratization. Whether they succeed may become one of the decisive political questions of the next phase. Kurdish Opinion The majority of Kurds support the “process.” Yet this should not be confused with trust in Erdoğan. They are carefully observing how the law will be implemented. It is moving beyond rhetoric into legislation; there is reason to hope for an end to the armed conflict, the release of prisoners, and the normalization of political life. Yet there still remains the memory of the collapse of the previous peace process of 2013–15, and the ongoing reality of trustee-controlled municipalities, mass prosecutions, and the weaponization of the judiciary against those calling for Kurdish rights. Therefore, if Kurds are turning their faces toward peace, this by no means implies that they are opening their minds to Erdoğan’s autocracy. They have learned a bitter lesson: if they don’t empower themselves, they will remain powerless. The continuing repression of Yeni Parti municipalities creates an intense dilemma within the Kurdish constituency. A Kurdish voter may simultaneously believe that Öcalan is right to pursue negotiations, that ending the armed conflict is historically necessary, and that the government’s treatment of the Yeni Parti is fundamentally undemocratic. The methods now used against the Yeni Parti — criminal investigations, removal of elected officials, prolonged detention, and politicized prosecutions — closely resemble those long directed against Kurdish municipalities. Rather than drawing Kurdish politics toward Erdoğan, this may reinforce a different conclusion: negotiations can end the war, but democratic guarantees must become universal. The government’s current perspectives and actual governance give no hint of democratic transformation. They are best understood as a set of selective nonaggression pacts under a wider authoritarianism. The state is relaxing one historic axis of coercion while intensifying another. Armed conflict has long vanished from the former war zone between Turkey and the PKK. The decisive question is no longer whether there will be armed conflict or whether the PKK leaves the mountains. The issue, now, is whether the political room opened by the call to lay arms becomes a democratic space for all or merely space newly monopolized by Erdoğan’s state and his military-industrial complex.

articles.title: Israel kills son of Gaza health official in latest atrocities
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Footage flooded the internet on Saturday, September 19, showing Gaza Health Ministry Director General Dr. Munir al-Bursh asking young men to bring the rest of his son’s body as they carried his remains. “Bring me his other half!” the grief-stricken father said. “We were supposed to go to heaven together today, but you got there before me, son.” According to media reports , Dr. Munir’s son, Bashir (28), was struck by a drone shortly after leaving his family’s tent in the al-Zahra neighborhood, near the Civil Defense headquarters, west of the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza Strip. Bashir was targeted while helping people fill their water containers, just meters away from his father. For many, the proximity of Dr. Munir implies that he, too, may have been a target of the attack. Israel’s systematic targeting of health workers The prominent Palestinian health official has been in the crosshairs of the Israeli forces since the beginning of Israel’s genocidal aggression on Gaza, due to his leading role in managing a crumbling health system that was severely devastated during the war. Moreover, Dr. Al-Bursh is widely known for frequently reporting on Israeli assaults on the Gaza medical sector, and highlighting the dire conditions of medical facilities inside the besieged areas via international media outlets. Al-Bursh and his family were previously targeted by Israeli warplanes at the very beginning of the war. In December 2023, his 13-year-old daughter, Jinan , was killed in an Israeli airstrike on a residential building in Jabalia. The aerial attack also resulted in the injury of Dr. Munir and the rest of his family. The deaths of Bashir and Jinan al-Bursh echo the murder of 15-year-old Ibrahim Abu Safiya by an Israeli drone in October 2024. Ibrahim was the son of the former director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya. Read more: ‘They brought me here to kill me,’ Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya tells lawyer The day Bashir al-Bursh was assassinated, and the days that followed, saw the killing of several people by the Israeli Army across different parts of the war-ravaged enclave. This took place as world leaders addressed the UN General Assembly. For the third year in a row, these addresses and the deliberations have failed to stop Israel’s aggression against Gaza and its ongoing heinous crimes carried out across West Asia.

articles.title: “New Low in U.N. History”: Trita Parsi on Trump’s Threat to Annihilate Iran at General Assembly
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. ANJALI KAMAT : At the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Secretary-General António Guterres reiterated his call for peace in the Middle East. SECRETARY - GENERAL ANTÓNIO GUTERRES : Across the Middle East, conflicts are cascading. So-called ceasefires have amounted to little more than lesser fires, with civilians continuing to pay the price. Enough is enough. I appeal to the leaders in this chamber to maximize this high-level week for deescalation and dialogue. And together, let’s send a clear message from this hall: The fighting must stop. AMY GOODMAN : Shortly after the secretary-general spoke before the United Nations General Assembly, President Trump took to the stage and openly threatened to annihilate Iran. PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : But I have a big decision to make: Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world, or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations? But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election, because it doesn’t make sense for them not to. They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already and won in a landslide. We won in a giant landslide, and I’ll be here for two-and-a-half years. ANJALI KAMAT : Trump’s remarks came as U.S. and Iranian officials met privately for three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and his Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff took part in the talks. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian told reporters that Iran is wary of further negotiations, having twice been attacked by the U.S. and Israel in the middle of talks. Pezeshkian will be addressing the United Nations today. During his speech on Tuesday, President Trump also boasted about seizing Venezuela’s oil after the U.S. attacked Venezuela and abducted President Nicolás Maduro and his wife PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : We signed the largest oil deal in history, covering 65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously and help drive down the cost of energy all over the world. And that is starting to perk right now. It’s coming out. The biggest oil companies in the world are going in, and the numbers are absolutely incredible. When you add the United States and Venezuela together, we have more than 60% of the oil in the world. So it’s perhaps the biggest deal. It was a war, but it’s perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils. You’ve all heard that. AMY GOODMAN : Well, for more on Trump’s U.N. speech, we’re joined now by Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. Trita, welcome to our studio here in New York, your first time here, as you deal with the U.N. General Assembly this week. Can you first start off by talking about Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran? TRITA PARSI : This is unfortunately the language that Trump keeps on using. I think, in his mind, it gives him the impression or leaves the impression that he’s in control of the situation, that he’s dictating terms, that he is winning. I don’t think that is how it is read by others. I think the Iranians see this, and I think they said so as much, that this is a sign of his desperation, because seven months into this war, there still is no exit, and Trump is increasingly facing what could end up becoming an endless war. And he has not achieved a single one of his strategic objectives. And the more the situation gets bad, the harsher his rhetoric tends to become. But this is probably a new low in U.N. history to actually have a president, a head of state, threatening the annihilation of another regime at the podium in the General Assembly. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Trita, just a few hours after making these comments threatening to annihilate Iran, President Trump also told reporters that his negotiating team had a very good three-hour meeting with the Iranian team. What do we know about that meeting? What was discussed? TRITA PARSI : So, this is something that the Qataris, in particular, had worked very, very hard to broker. It was an indirect meeting, so they were not sitting in the same room, even though they had been in the past. So, there is a slight return to diplomacy, but it is not at the same level as it was before, in which the two sides were talking directly to each other. But it is nevertheless an important attempt of bringing the two sides back to the table. But it does not appear to have generated any real breakthrough. The two sides are too far away from each other on substantive issues, it appears. Nevertheless, attempts of this kind are very important. They have to be made. You’re not going to have a breakthrough unless you try some of these small steps. But I do fear that, to a certain extent, this is also in order to give the impression that more is happening diplomatically than it actually is because of the impact it has on the markets, because expectations it sets for the midterm elections. But in reality, in terms of substance, I’m not seeing any breakthrough, not quite yet. ANJALI KAMAT : The Iranian president is expected to address the United Nations General Assembly today. What do you think he’s going to be talking about? And what exactly is happening in the Strait of Hormuz? TRITA PARSI : So, in the Strait of Hormuz, you do have a situation in which the United States has managed to open up the southern channel, in which more oil is flowing now than it did during the MOU , or at least in the early days of the MOU . This, I think, has led to a scenario in which the United States thinks that the tables have been turned, that the pressure is much higher on Iran now than it is on the global economy. To a certain extent, that is true, but here’s the problem: It is not a stable situation. If these new sanctions that Trump is pushing for, including this opening in the strait, actually really ends up putting a lot of pressure on the Iranians, what you’re most likely to see in that scenario is that the Iranians will counter-escalate. The United States is currently escalating. It is trying to ban all airplanes from landing in Iran or all Iranian airlines from being able to go to other places. These are clear escalations of added pressure. And if those end up biting, the Iranians will counter-escalate. So we’re not in a situation in which the United States is putting added pressure on a country that has run out of options. It’s adding pressure on a country that has plenty of escalatory options, and most of those are very dangerous for the region and for the United States itself. And as a result, this trajectory is one of escalation, despite that meeting that took place yesterday. AMY GOODMAN : It was quite something to hear President Trump say, essentially, the U.S. has obliterated Iran’s military, the Navy. He claimed Operation Midnight Hammer obliterated Iran’s nuclear program, so wiping out everything. Yet, then, why is — well, according to polls in the United States across the political spectrum, people perceive the U.S. is losing against Iran. And what don’t we know about the level of devastation of U.S. bases throughout the Middle East right now? TRITA PARSI : I think the American public actually sees reality for what it is, and it is a situation in which the United States, after seven months of fighting, have not been able to achieve any of its objectives and, even more importantly, finding an exit out of this war. So, all of this talk about destroying their Navy, etc., there are tactical operational successes that the United States has had; none of them have translated into a strategic victory. And even this latest maneuver, in which the U.S. thinks that he has managed to get an edge over the Iranians in terms of leverage, which to a certain extent may be true, is nevertheless a tactical edge, not a strategic edge. And this constant confusing, deliberate confusing, between what is tactical and strategic is what has really characterized how the administration has approached this. Now, when it comes to the U.S. bases, General David Petraeus, former head of the CIA , himself admitted that the Iranians have made a majority of American bases in the region inoperable. The United States is actually not even operating out of a lot of these bases at this point because of the success and effectiveness of the Iranian missiles and the lack of effectiveness of the missile defense. The U.S. is running out of interceptors, etc. So the picture on the ground is dramatically different from what the president is conveying. ANJALI KAMAT : Trita, Trump claimed in his speech that Iran is watching the midterms very closely. What is Iran’s calculation if the Democrats end up winning? And what do you think the Democrats should do on Iran if they do win? TRITA PARSI : I think the Iranians are looking at the midterms, but it’s not that decisive moment necessarily that earlier was thought. I think the Iranians are also understanding that if Trump loses in the elections both the House and the Senate, he will be in a much more desperate situation. He will be facing domestic pressure, perhaps impeachment efforts. And that may very well end up causing him to lash out even more on the foreign policy front. Instead of that constraining him, it actually may further radicalize his policies. So, I don’t think they’re looking at the midterms necessarily as something that is some sort of a decisive blow towards Trump, and as a result, things wind down. Now, I do believe that the Democrats could do far more in terms of putting pressure to stop this war, stop the funding of this war. Now there’s efforts in terms of war powers, etc. Some of them have been successful. But at the end of the day, it’s the power of the purse. And also, when the MOU was signed, however imperfect it may have been, I found it tremendously problematic that many of the Democrats were choosing to attack the MOU in a manner that could have led, and eventually did lead, not necessarily because of their attacks, to the MOU collapsing. And what did that do? It brought us back into war. So, you have to really decide. If you’re against this war, you have to support the efforts that ends these wars, whether those are perfect or not, and save the political scores later on until we’re completely safe, out of the woods, and we don’t have a fear of a return to military action. AMY GOODMAN : Where does China fit into this picture? A lot is being made of President Trump’s meeting with Xi this week in New York. Whether we’ll get to hear what they say is another story, because the pool, the media pool, has said they won’t operate, in solidarity with the networks that have been banned from the White House. CNN is part of the pool, and so they’re just saying, “We won’t record.” TRITA PARSI : The meeting tomorrow is going to be very important. The United States is going to try to press the Chinese to go along with extraterritorial sanctions as part of this economic warfare that the administration is now waging and escalating. I find it unlikely — AMY GOODMAN : The U.S. almost bombed a Chinese ship. Is that right? And then at the last minute, as they were ready to bomb this Chinese ship, saying that they had intelligence that it was bringing weapons or nuclear material to Iran, realized it was based on AI that was false. TRITA PARSI : Exactly, and we’ve already seen mistakes be committed because of this overreliance on AI. The AI program that was developed by Palantir is partly responsible for the bombing of the girls’ school in Minab that left 150-plus children dead. During the first round of the war back in March, I spoke to a person in Iran who said that it appears that AI is being used for a lot of the targeting decisions. For instance, there was a period in that war in which the United States and Israel were specifically targeting police stations. This was during the phase in which I think the United States and Israel hoped that by destroying the security forces in the city, it would lead to riots and an overthrow of the government. But it also led to them bombing twice a park that is called Park Police, Pārk-e Pelis in Persian, had nothing to do with the police, but because of the name “police” is in the name of the park, it was targeted. And it appears to have been yet another one of these examples in which the AI is selecting the targets without any human oversight to just double-check, triple-check if this is valid or not. And you just raised the worst example so far in terms of actually a potential war between the U.S. and China. Now, it’s interesting. The Chinese at some point may decide that they might want to get in and try to see if they can help bring this war to an end. It’s not usually what they want to do. Their instincts are to stay out. But if this situation escalates further, to the point in which the Chinese cannot insulate themselves and the global economy from the repercussions, the Chinese calculation may change. And it may also come as a result of the pressure that the U.S. is putting on the Chinese to go along with sanctions that they absolutely do not want to implement. ANJALI KAMAT : And the significance, Trita, you know, when President Trump was talking about Venezuela, of his comment saying, “To the victor belongs the spoils,” speaking to the U.N. General Assembly? TRITA PARSI : Yes, it’s really important to understand this point here. The entire U.N. system was built upon the ashes of the world after World War II, in which it was deemed critical by all of the states that we need to move towards a different type of a system in which warfare should not pay off, in which the victors do not go — the spoils do not go to the victor, because there shouldn’t be any benefit in waging wars, particularly the wars of aggression and wars of choice. So, for him to come with that statement, that probably is mainly meant to play well with a specific audience at home, nevertheless sends a strong message to the rest of the world that the United States, at least currently, does not even deem the most basic principles of international law as something that is worthy to uphold. AMY GOODMAN : Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. Coming up, Senator Bernie Sanders gave a major address this week at the historic Riverside Church in New York on war, oligarchy and the dangers of AI. Stay with us. articles.title: Bernie Sanders: The World Is “Moving in the Wrong Direction” on War, Climate, Inequality & AI Tech
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat. ANJALI KAMAT : As world leaders are gathering in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly, Senator Bernie Sanders gave a major address in New York on Monday. He spoke at the historic Riverside Church, where Martin Luther King gave his “Beyond Vietnam” speech on April 4th, 1967, exactly one year before he was assassinated. In that speech, King spoke against racism, militarism and materialism. AMY GOODMAN : These are some of the excerpts from Senator Bernie Sanders’ speech. SEN . BERNIE SANDERS : What Dr. King said was true nearly 60 years ago, and it is even truer today, as our country, the United States of America, is now spending over a trillion dollars a year on the military, while some 800,000 Americans are homeless, 85 million Americans are uninsured or underinsured, and millions of people cannot afford the basic necessities of life. And this business of spending more and more on the military and turning backs on working families and the poor is not just happening tragically here in the United States. It’s happening all over the world, where we are seeing increased military budgets while the needs of people living in desperation are ignored. So, not just in the United States, but all over the world, we are moving in the wrong direction, and our job is to turn that around. Instead of producing more bombs and weapons and seeing the military-industrial complex enjoy huge profits, governments throughout the world need to come together to feed the children, take care of the vulnerable and protect our planet from the ravages of climate change. And that is why we must continue and accelerate our efforts to end Trump’s disastrous war in Iran, which is now spreading throughout the region. That is why we must continue to speak out against the extremist government in Israel and the genocide they have committed in Gaza, and why we in the United States must end all military aid to the Netanyahu government. And that is — and that is why we must rally and work with grassroots activists in Russia to put an end to Putin’s disastrous war in Ukraine, which has led — not widely known, not widely reported, but has led to the deaths of some 500,000 Russian soldiers, as well as mass destruction and loss of life in Ukraine. And that is why we must denounce the United Arab Emirates’ continued financial and military support of the RSF as it wages a campaign of genocide and destruction in Sudan’s civil war. … While the billionaire class and the 1% have never, ever had it so good, over 60% of Americans, in the richest country in the history of the world, are living paycheck to paycheck, nearly 800,000 are homeless, and tens of millions struggle to pay for rent or mortgage or keep a roof over their heads. And let us be very clear: The rapid movement to oligarchy and the exponential rise in income and wealth inequality is not just an American phenomenon. It is taking place all over the world and, in my view, is the most important economic reality of our times. In country after country, what we are seeing is working people sick and tired of seeing the very rich get richer while they struggle to put food on the table and pay for basic necessities. … But it is not just income and wealth inequality and concentration of ownership that we are seeing today. Literally today, billionaires are determined to own our political system, as well. In the United States, as a result of the disastrous Citizens United Supreme Court decision, billionaires and corporations are legally able to spend as much as they want on political campaigns through their super PACs. And that, my friends, is exactly what they are doing right at this moment. In the last election, presidential election, Mr. Musk spent at least $290 million to elect Trump as president, and now he is spending some $200 million more to help Republicans keep control over the Congress. And it’s not just Republican billionaires; there are Democratic billionaires who are also playing an important role. … As the U.N. secretary-general reminded us, there’s another issue that we must confront. In my view, artificial intelligence, AI, and robotics are the most transformational technologies in the history of humanity. They have the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs. They threaten the privacy — AI threatens the privacy of virtually every person in this world through mass surveillance. Every phone call you make, every website you visit, every email that you send, somebody will know it. … It is advancing exponentially. In under four years, we have gone from an AI that could barely write a coherent tweet to AI systems that have already escaped the control of the companies that built them. Take a deep breath and ask yourself: Where will AI be in two years, in four years, in 10 years? Will human beings be able to control this exploding technology? So, let me make a very radical suggestion. And that is, if the lives of every man, woman and child are going to be fundamentally changed by this technology, then the people of our country and the people of this world must make the decisions regarding AI, not just a handful of Big Tech oligarchs. And that is why I hope very much that when President Trump and President Xi meet on Thursday, I hope very much that they will sit down and begin the process of negotiating a comprehensive treaty to establish a pause on advanced AI and a ban on AI superintelligence. AMY GOODMAN : Vermont’s democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders speaking at Riverside Church in New York on Monday.

articles.title: Nepali Activist at U.N. Rally Calls for Climate Justice After Deadly Glacier Floods Kill Thousands
articles.content: In the wake of devastating flash floods triggered by glacial collapse in the Himalayas, Nepal is demanding climate reparations from polluter countries as it embarks upon the grueling process of rebuilding. Over 1,400 bodies have been recovered from the disaster, with around 6,000 others still missing. Nepal’s government estimates that the cost of infrastructure reconstruction is likely to exceed $4 billion. Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global carbon emissions, yet as a mountainous country surrounded by glaciers, continues to be vulnerable to the effects of climate change. Recent studies estimate that global surface temperatures will likely exceed 1.5°C above preindustrial levels by the end of the decade. We go to a rally outside of United Nations headquarters, where Nepali activists, including our guest Anisha Buda, are demanding climate justice, reparations and a just transition out of fossil fuels. Buda, a member of the region’s ethnic minority Kaike-speaking Magar community, says that almost 90% of the victims impacted by August’s flash flooding were part of Nepal’s Indigenous communities. “It is not just the lives of the people lost. It’s not just the houses swept, but it’s their culture, tradition and their very identity that is being lost by the floods, by the climate-induced disasters.”

articles.title: “Secretary of Measlesland”: Dr. Paul Offit Slams RFK Jr.’s Handling of Deadly Measles Outbreak
articles.content: 2026 is already the deadliest year for measles in the United States since the virus was declared eliminated in 2000. Four people died over the last month in Pennsylvania amid an ongoing outbreak in the state, which had not seen a measles-related death in at least 35 years. All four victims, including two infants, were unvaccinated (children do not receive their first dose of the measles vaccine until they have reached a year old). The deaths come as President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. continue to defund public vaccination programs and push debunked claims that vaccines cause autism. Pediatrician and vaccine expert Dr. Paul Offit warns that the four reported measles deaths — which were reported by Pennsylvania health officials but have not yet been acknowledged by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — are likely a vast undercount. He estimates that there could be “closer to 4,000” cases in the Pennsylvania outbreak. “I don’t think people realize how contagious this virus is,” Offit says. “You don’t have to have direct contact with somebody who has measles. You just have to be within their airspace within two hours of them being there.” We also speak to Offit about the COVID -19 virus, which he says is now affecting the United States “like flu” by causing “hundreds of thousands of people to be hospitalized and tens of thousands to die, just like influenza does, every year.” Yearly flu and COVID -19 vaccinations, he explains, are “effective at keeping people out of the hospital, effective at keeping them out of the intensive care unit, and effective at keeping them out of the morgue.”

articles.title: ICE shoots Texas delivery driver, then detains him with bullet lodged in his back
articles.author: Devin B. Martinez
articles.content: Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a food delivery driver in North Austin, Texas, was shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents while he was making a delivery on Sunday, September 20. Garces Perez, who survived the shooting but is now partially paralyzed, says his car was rammed by a large black unmarked truck. ICE claimed they attempted a traffic stop and that Garces Perez fled, but the DoorDash driver and his lawyers’ account contradict this report, saying after he tried to U-turn and pullover, ICE agents rammed his vehicle again, and then an agent got out and aimed his weapon through the passenger side of the car and shot Garces Perez in the back of his neck. CBP revealed on Tuesday, September 22, that the officer that fired the shot was not wearing a body camera, despite the agency’s body-camera requirements. After a few hours in the hospital, Garces Perez was transferred to ICE custody with the bullet still lodged in his back . “I am not doing well due to the gunshot wound and I have not received the medical attention that I require,” he said through a translator at a press conference in Austin. After receiving no pain medication at the hospital, Garces Perez said that in ICE custody, he was forced to sleep on the floor and repeatedly asked for medical care while in severe pain. His attorney also said he developed paralysis on his left side. Local community demands ICE out of Austin Within hours of the shooting, protests erupted in Austin . Hundreds of residents flooded the streets demanding ICE out of their neighborhoods. Organizers have connected the shooting to a growing number of fatal and nonfatal encounters involving immigration agents, including the killings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Ruben Ray Martinez in South Padre Island. “We cannot be silent as ICE is shooting and killing our neighbors!” a statement by the Austin branch of the Party for Socialism and Liberation said. Protests have continued across Austin on Monday and Tuesday. Student walkouts were also seen on Tuesday, September 22, by students across Pflugerville, Texas, north of downtown Austin, as well as Navarro Early College High School. DHS defends the shooting and promises to investigate After the shooting, the Department of Homeland Security quickly claimed that Garces Perez was an “illegal alien from Venezuela, who illegally entered” the United States. Garces Perez’s lawyers have refuted these claims , saying he entered the country through CBP One, the US border processing system. “He had a work permit. He was seeking asylum.” They said that a notice of hearing was sent to an old address, despite Garces Perez updating his address with the immigration court. “He didn’t know he had a hearing. So he didn’t go and got a deportation order in absentia, which is a very common thing.” According to reports, DHS and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) are leading an investigation into the ICE shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez. Austin police and the Travis County district attorney’s office have also said they intend to investigate the shooting. But their investigations come amid strong criticism of federal officials’ handling of previous ICE shootings in Texas. In Houston, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare has said federal officials did not provide his office with information about the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. He is taking his own investigation to a grand jury to force the release of more details. ICE violence continues in the US The Austin shooting follows a series of fatal encounters involving federal immigration agents this year, including the killings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. As federal agents continue to face scrutiny over deadly encounters in Texas and other states, Austin residents and organizers say they will continue protesting and organizing until ICE is out of their communities.
